DescriptionLong.0x00004953:
The FT-86 Concept was introduced in 2009 to the delight of Japanese sports car enthusiasts everywhere. The exciting front-engine/rear-drive sports car was developed by a collaborative effort between Toyota and Subaru, and it rekindled the spirit of the legendary Toyota AE86. In 2011, the production version of the FT-86 made its long-awaited debut at the Tokyo Motor Show.

The "FT" (Future Toyota) designation was dropped, going simply by the name Toyota 86. The new-generation "Hachi-Roku" (86 in Japanese) featured a profile similar to that of the FT-86 II Concept shown at the 2011 Geneva Motor Show. The sleek body adopted Toyota's "Aero Handling" concept, which was the company's advanced aerodynamic philosophy.

Under the hood was a naturally-aspirated 1998cc DOHC flat-4, or "boxer" engine, mounted aft of the front axle. It produced an even <200ps> at <7000rpm> and <20.9kgm> of torque at <6600rpm>. The power was transferred to the rear wheels via a 6-speed manual gearbox or a 6-speed automatic transmission with paddle shifters. Its ideal 53:47 front/rear weight distribution allowed for true sports car handling, with some models getting a limited-slip differential for even more precise cornering. Another reason for the car's amazing agility was because its center of gravity was located in the same place as many exotic supercars, sitting only <460mm> off the ground. The car was also lightweight, tipping the scales at <1230kg>.

Tuning firms, such as Modelista and TRD, offered plenty of customization for the 86, and they showed us that it made for a excellent starting point to build a race car. In sum, the 86 was a lightweight sports car that truly catered to the young car enthusiast of its day.N
DescriptionLong.0x00004958:
The DTM (Deutsche Tourenwagen Meisterschaft) series allowed significant vehicle upgrades in 1993, leading to DTM cars with a wide variety of electronic control devices like ABS. The cars featured such high levels of technology that they were often referred to as "F1 in a box."

The Alfa Romeo 155 entered the DTM in 1993 and experienced success right off the bat, trouncing the formidable AMG Mercedes-Benz 190E to win its maiden race. It won 12 of 20 races that year, taking home both the Drivers' and Manufacturers' Championships. This car, known as the 155 2.5 V6 TI, was built based on the 155 sedan that appeared in 1992. The 2.5-liter 60-degree V-6 generated <420ps>, which was sent to all four wheels.

In 1995, the 155 adopted a 6-speed sequential paddle-shift semi-automatic, similar to those used by Formula 1 cars, but it wasn't enough to beat the up-and-coming Mercedes-Benz teams that year. In 1996, Alfa entered with a new 90-degree V-type engine that put out <490ps>. As a result, the 155 took 10 wins in 26 races at 13 events, besting both Mercedes-Benz (7 wins) and Opel (9 wins). However, the 155 lagged behind in points and left without retaking the title. At the end of the season, the DTM series integrated with the ITC, and the DTM was gone, for a while.

Interestingly, an Alfa Romeo 155 2.5 V6 TI was driven by former F1 driver Alessandro Nannini, whose right arm was severed in a helicopter accident in 1990. Nannini's 155 was equipped with separate gear levers that allowed him to shift with one arm.C
DescriptionLong.0x00004959:
The Nissan 180SX — sold as the Nissan 240SX in the U.S. and the 200SX in the EU — was created as the Silvia's sister hatchback model in March 1989. This car, sporting retractable headlights and a glass hatchback, was overshadowed by the coupe at first—despite sharing the same powerplant, a 1.8-liter DOHC inline-4 that came available only with a turbocharger. But as time went on, people recognized the true value of this stylish sports coupe and sales began to climb.

The engine received an upgrade in 1991 to the SR20DET, the same 2.0-liter DOHC inline-4 in the normal Silvia with output rated at <205ps> and <28.0kgm>. This prolonged the 180SX's life span because its production run was initially slated to end alongside the S13 Silvia; however, thanks to the popularity of the 2.4-liter 240SX in the U.S. (that possessed the same body shape of 180SX), Nissan elected to keep the compact rear-drive coupe around.

In 1996, the first normally-aspirated 180SX, the Type S, was added to the lineup. Without forced induction, the Type S lacked the acceleration of the hotter version. This made the car a favorite among tuners, who took things into their own hands, giving the car their own dose of power and beefing the chassis up accordingly. This paved the way for a new 180SX, one that featured the Silvia's front end, making the two cars virtual clones of each other; it was dubbed the "Sil-Eighty."
DescriptionLong.0x0000495A:
Called Japan’s first exotic or supercar by some, the Toyota 2000GT was certainly revolutionary as far as Japanese cars went. The smooth, flowing lines of the 2000GT were reminiscent of European super cars of the day, and it was built on a backbone chassis.

Underneath its long hood was a 2.0-liter DOHC inline-6, based on the top-of-the-line Crown powerplant, which produced <150ps>. This engine was jointly developed by Yamaha. The famous motorcycle/musical instrument maker also provided the wood grain on the car’s dashboard with materials it used for its world-class pianos.

The car’s suspension was also first rate, with double wishbones at both front and rear. But the Toyota 2000GT was not all about beauty. This highly tuned machine was able to win several times on the Fuji Speedway and Suzuka circuit, even establishing the international speed record on the Yatabe test course going as fast as <220km/h>. Two special convertible versions were produced for the James Bond movie, “You Only Live Twice,” giving the Toyota sports car worldwide appeal.

Sales of such a high-end sports car were not stellar, especially one with a price tag of 2,380,000 yen, which was twice as expensive as the luxury model Crown, and Toyota was faced with the hard reality of ceasing the car’s production after making only 300 cars.
DescriptionLong.0x0000495B:
The 208 GTi is the high-performance variant of the 208, Peugeot’s mainstream compact car. It made its official debut at the Paris Motor Show in the fall of 2012, following the launch of the new 208 series earlier that spring.

A key development goal for the 208 series was to redefine Peugeot’s B-segment offering, addressing the issue of the 207 becoming too large and heavy. While the 208 retained the 207’s platform, its overall length was reduced to less than <4m> by trimming the front and rear overhangs. Also, the use of lighter materials resulted in a <100kg> weight reduction compared to its predecessor.

This weight-saving effort particularly benefited the GTi model. It allowed Peugeot to rekindle the spirit of the legendary 205 GTI—a globally acclaimed sports model known for its compact size, agility, and thrilling performance.

Visually, the 208 GTi featured subtle yet distinctive enhancements, including a large roof spoiler, 18-inch wheels, and unique trim elements. Beneath the surface, however, significant engineering refinements were made. The front and rear track widths were widened by <10mm> and <20mm>, respectively, while the suspension, subframe, and control arms were specifically tuned for this model.

Power came from a turbocharged 1.6-liter inline-4 direct-injection engine, producing <200ps>/<28.0kgm>, paired with a 6-speed manual gearbox.

With a top speed of <230km/h> and a 0-<100 km/h> acceleration time of 6.8 seconds, it was among the hottest hatches in its class.-
DescriptionLong.0x0000495C:
Styled by Pininfarina, the 250 GT Berlinetta made its debut at the 1959 Paris Motor Show, equipped with a 3.0-liter 12-cylinder engine that had 250 cc of displacement in each of its cylinders, as the name implied.

There was a definitive difference between this car and previous models. The car's wheelbase, which measured <2600mm> long, had been chopped down to <2400mm> in order to improve cornering agility. It was also to give it an edge in GT category racing. Years later, the car came to be known as the "250 GT Berlinetta passo corto," or 250 GT Berlinetta SWB (the abbreviation for Short Wheelbase in English) to distinguish this version from previous models.

The 250 GT Berlinetta passo corto began production in 1960, a year after its public unveiling, and came with an all-aluminum racing body, as well as a steel body for road-going models. The <2953cc> SOHC V12 produced between <220ps> to <280ps>, depending on its degree of tuning, and was the first mass production vehicle by Ferrari to be equipped with 4-wheel disc brakes.

The immediate racing success that was to follow was largely attributed to the car's shorter wheelbase: Nearly unstoppable, it won the Tour De France Automobile three years in a row from 1960 to 1962 and the GT category at Le Mans in 1960 and 1961. It also won the Nürburgring <1000km> race two years in a row, from 1961 to 1962. Thereafter, the 250 GT passed the baton to the 250 GTO, which was based on the 250 GT Berlinetta passo corto. In the end, only 162 examples of this beautiful grand touring machine were built.
DescriptionLong.0x0000495D:
When you think of multi-million-dollar classic exotics, the first name that usually comes to mind is Ferrari. And among all the valuable Ferrari cars through history, the 250 GTO stands out as the “collectable Ferrari.” Built in the early 1960s, the 250 GTO, the original Testarossa, made an immediate impact on the world sports car scene.

The “250” in the name indicates its engine displacement of 250cc per cylinder. And the car had 12 cylinders, which meant it was a total displacement of 3.0 liters. The “GTO” stands for Gran Turismo Omologato, a reference to it being a homologation model for GT racing. And as such a name implies, it was introduced in 1962 specifically to win the GT class in international production sports car racing.

The car was based on the agile 250 GT SWB, but with a lighter curb weight. Covering its steel tubular frame was an all-aluminum body, and the nose was long and low in order to boost aerodynamic performance. The rear of the car was characterized by a coda tronca, with bulging rear fenders to allow space for large tires. The ride height of the car is <90mm> lower than the SWB. Power comes from a Testarossa engine with a dry oil sump and six carburetors, delivering an output of <300ps>. It helped enable the car to reach a top speed of <300km/h>.

Only 39 250 GTOs were ever produced, which by itself was not enough for homologation. But Ferrari stated that the car was simply a variation of the SWB, and once this was accepted, the car started racing in '62. The 250 GTO won the international championship three years in a row.

All 39 of these cars still exist today. The 3729GT included in the game is a right-hand drive model delivered to the UK in '62. It was once raced by a Ferrari semi-works team, and achieved podium finishes in many British races. 8
DescriptionLong.0x0000495E:
With the introduction of the Group B category in 1982, a number of auto makers brought new limited-run super sports cars to the market. This was because in order to compete in the Group B class, 200 units of production cars based on the race car were required to be produced. One of these cars was the Ferrari GTO, which bowed at the 1984 Geneva Motor Show. Some people referred to this car as the 288 GTO, although it is not the car's official name.

The "O" in GTO stands for omologazione, the Italian word for homologation. Upon first glance, it is obvious that the GTO gets its styling cues from the classic 308 GTB, but despite their similar looks, the GTO was an entirely different beast altogether. Unlike the 308 GTB, it featured a longitudinally-mounted engine, a <110mm> longer wheelbase, and body panels made from carbon fiber and other lightweight materials. 

Leonardo Fioravanti, who was with Pininfarina at the time, penned the exterior styling. Flared front and rear fenders, additional fog lights, passing lights in the nose, a rear duck tail reminiscent of the 250 GTO, and three-lined louvers gave the GTO a wonderful balance of aggressiveness and elegance. Power came from a revamped Lancia LC2 engine, which was turned from a naturally-aspirated 3.0-liter to a twin-turbocharged 2.6-liter, then later into a 2.8-liter, the maximum displacement allowed in Group B. With <400ps> and <50.6kgm> of torque on tap, the <1160kg> sports car was the fastest Ferrari in its day, with a top speed of <305km/h>. 

Only 272 examples of the 288 GTO were manufactured, and it never actually ran a race. The GTO eventually led to the development of the 288 GTO Evoluzione test vehicle, which in turn became the foundation for the now-legendary F40.
DescriptionLong.0x0000495F:
AMG began as a company that designed and tested race engines, founded by two engineers from Daimler-Benz’s development department. The company created this Mercedes-Benz 300 SEL 6.8 AMG for touring car races. 

The stock 300 SEL 6.3 was powered by a 6.3-liter V-8. The car was plenty fast, but AMG decided to push the envelope even further by increasing the engine's displacement to 6.8 liters, adding special cams and other dedicated parts developed in-house to raise output from <250ps> to <428ps>. In 1971, the car won its class in the 1971 Spa Francorchamps 24 Hour race, and came in 2nd place overall. 

It is said that only a total of three race cars and two test cars were ever produced.
DescriptionLong.0x00004960:
At the 1955 New York International Auto Show, Daimler-Benz unveiled an innovative new sports car—the Mercedes-Benz 300 SL. Its engine was mounted longitudinally within a lightweight multi-tubular space frame crafted from slender steel pipes, and tilted at a 50-degree angle to allow for the lowest possible hood line. Equipped with a 4-speed transmission, this high-performance machine was capable of reaching speeds of up to <260km/h>.

The car’s most distinctive features were its unique side doors. They opened upward and were hinged at the center of the roof. When both doors were raised, the car’s silhouette resembled a seagull in flight—earning the 300 SL’s doors the famous moniker, "gullwing."

Power came from a <2996cc> SOHC inline-6 engine, the first production engine to employ the same mechanical fuel injection system used in the W196 Formula 1 racer. This setup produced an impressive <215ps> at <5800rpm>. Although its 4-wheel drum brakes and <1295kg> curb weight were considerable for the time, the car’s exceptional engine performance made it one of the preeminent sports cars of its era. The production 300 SL proved its worth on the track as well, securing numerous victories in sports-car racing.

Between 1955 and 1957, 1,400 300 SL gullwing coupes were built. In 1957, production of the coupe ended, passing the torch to the 300 SL Roadster, an open-top successor that continued the legacy of one of Mercedes-Benz’s most iconic creations.
DescriptionLong.0x00004961:
When thinking of Ferrari's motorsports activities, the first thing that comes to mind are their feats in the F1 Grand Prix. However from the 1950s to the 1960s, they also enjoyed great success in sports car racing. Though they withdrew from sports car racing in 1973, the 330 P4 is one car that left its name in history for being the most beautiful machine out of the "P series" V12 midship engine prototype racers, that left a glorious record from the '60s to the '70s.

330 stands for the displacement per cylinder, in other words signifying a 4-liter displacement engine, and the name stands for the fourth version of the P series equipped with a 4-liter engine.

The 330 P4 debuting in 1967 was developed by improving upon the 330 P3, in order to defeat the Ford GT which was on top at the time. Though with the same displacement as the previous version, it was given a <450ps> engine of an almost brand new design, with 3 valves per cylinder consisting of two intake and 1 exhaust on the heads. The nose of the body was slightly extended to the front, and a separate spoiler was added to the rear, to improve its aerodynamic capabilities.

In actual racing, it started off by winning its debut race in the 24 hours of Daytona, and in the Monza 1,000 km race. Unfortunately it was defeated by Ford in the 24 Hours of Le Mans, but it was successful in defeating Porsche in the sports car world championships, and became series champion.
DescriptionLong.0x00004962:
The Porsche 356, the German sports car maker's first mass-production model, made its debut in 1949. It went through major updates in 1955 and 1959. During these two updates, the car was referred to as the 356A.

The 356A was simply a modernized version of the original, with a rounded windshield, soft padding above the interior panels, and a horn at the center of the steering wheel. The performance of the 356A improved every year, which ultimately led to the creation of the 1500 GS Carrera and the 1500 GS GT Carrera, a pair of limited-production models that were in essence the GT3s of their day.

Power came from a slightly detuned version of the 4-cam engine found in the 550 Spyder race car. The 1500 GS Carrera, offered as the road-going model, produced <100ps>, while the track-ready 1500 GS GT Carrera pumped out <110ps>. The two cars came in the forms of a coupe, cabriolet, and speedster.

Of particular note is that these cars were the very first to carry the "Carrera" moniker, a name that has now become synonymous with Porsche. !
DescriptionLong.0x00004963:
Following the debut of the 1973 Berlinetta Boxer, Ferrari’s V-12-powered supercars transitioned to mid-engine layouts, which would define the marque’s flagship models for many years to come. The final front-engine rear-wheel-drive Ferrari before this hiatus was the 365 GTB4, more widely recognized by its popular nickname, “Daytona.”

The nickname stemmed from Ferrari’s commanding performance at the 1967 Daytona 24-hour race, where the 330 P4 and 412 P sports prototypes secured a 1-2-3 finish, sweeping the podium.

The first to reportedly refer to the car as the “Daytona” was Luigi Chinetti, owner of the Ferrari dealer and semi-works racing outfit, the North American Racing Team (N.A.R.T.), at the time of the prototype’s initial delivery.

The Daytona was developed with a strong focus on the North American market. Its sleek silhouette penned by Leonardo Fioravanti of Pininfarina. Initially fitted with quad headlights housed beneath Plexiglas covers, the design was updated to retractable units after 1970 to comply with North American safety regulations.

Under the hood, the <4390cc> DOHC V-12 engine was fed by six Weber carburetors, producing <352ps> and <44.0kgm> of torque. Its claimed top speed of <280km/h> matched that of its chief rival, the Lamborghini Miura, making it the fastest road car of its era.

At Daytona, it went on to dominate the Le Mans GT class for three consecutive years, cementing its legacy in motorsports history.
DescriptionLong.0x00004964:
With a new version of Ferrari's mid-engine V-8 car appearing every five years (starting from 1989), the successor to the popular F430 arrived in 2009. Called the Ferrari 458 Italia, the sleek supercar was introduced at the 2009 Frankfurt Motor Show, succeeding the likes of the 348 (1989), F355 (1994), 360 Modena (1999) and F430 (2004).

The 458 Italia was built upon a newly designed aluminum space frame, which made it lighter than its predecessor. Behind the cockpit resided a direct-injection V-8 that pumped out <570ps>/<55.1kgm>, astonishing figures from a normally-aspirated engine. Power was transferred to the rear wheels via a 7-speed dual-clutch gearbox whose shift speeds were significantly improved over the F355's. The Manettino system that unified the engine, gearbox, suspension, E-DIFF, F1 Trac, ESP and high-performance ABS controls was also improved, allowing the driver to choose one of five different modes: Low Grip, Sports, Race, CT cut, and CST cut.

The 458 Italia was a menace on the asphalt, running to <100km/h> in just 3.4 seconds, and hitting a top speed of <325km/h>. Considering that the final and very special grade model of the F430 Scuderia accelerated from 0 to <100km/h> in 3.6 seconds, and registered a top speed of <320km/h>, you can see the definite and distinct evolution in this Ferrari species.
DescriptionLong.0x00004965:
Many of Ferrari’s most memorable cars were powered by V-8 powerplants. Following in the footsteps of the 360 Modena and F430, the latest examples of these amazing V-8-powered machines is the 458 Italia. Designed and developed completely from scratch, the 458 Italia pays homage to the home country of Ferrari, christened by Ferrari’s then-chairman Luca Cordero di Montezemolo.

As with its predecessor, the main components of the 458 Italia’s chassis, body, engine, and suspension are composed of aluminum; however, the torsional rigidity of the 458 is improved by 15 percent when compared to the F430.

The body incorporates winglets inside the front grille and fender “chimney” outlets, allowing the 458 Italia to achieve amazing aerodynamic performance. The car produces <140kg> of downforce at <200km/h>, and more than <360kg> of downforce at top speed.

At the heart of the mid-engine/rear-drive machine is a fire-breathing 4.5-liter naturally-aspirated V-8 that produces <570ps> and <55.1kgm>. It comes mated to a dual-clutch 7-speed F1-matic gearbox whose shift speeds are on par with that of a F1 machine. The 458 Italia accelerates from 0-<100km/h> in 3.4 seconds and reaches a top speed of <325km/h>.

The on-road prowess of the supercar was so impressive that Ferrari decided to produce a race car version of it called the 458 Italia GT3.

The major changes made to the GT3 are to generate more downforce. The front bumper features a low air dam, while a large rear wing helps keep the rear tires planted to the driving surface. The car looks meaner than its production counterpart, thanks mainly to enlarged front and rear fenders. That said, engine power is a bit lower at <550ps> via a restrictor.

The car bowed in 2011 and won the series title that year in the FIA-GT European Championships.

The 458 Italia was built upon a newly designed aluminum space frame, which made it lighter than its predecessor. Behind the cockpit resided a direct-injection V-8 that pumped out <570ps>/<55.1kgm>, astonishing figures from a normally-aspirated engine. Power was transferred to the rear wheels via a 7-speed dual-clutch gearbox whose shift speeds were significantly improved over the F355's. The Manettino system that unified the engine, gearbox, suspension, E-DIFF, F1 Trac, ESP and high-performance ABS controls was also improved, allowing the driver to choose one of five different modes: Low Grip, Sports, Race, CT cut, and CST cut.

The 458 Italia was a menace on the asphalt, running to <100km/h> in just 3.4 seconds, and hitting a top speed of <325km/h>. Considering that the final and very special grade model of the F430 Scuderia accelerated from 0 to <100km/h> in 3.6 seconds, and registered a top speed of <320km/h>, you can see the definite and distinct evolution in this Ferrari species.

*This model was specially tuned to meet Gr.4 regulations by Gran Turismo.
DescriptionLong.0x00004967:
While Alfa Romeo produced a number of mid-engine race cars in its day, the 4C, introduced in 2013, represents the marque’s first mass-production car that features the performance-minded layout.

Alfa Romeo engineers stressed weight reduction when developing this high-performance sports car. They installed a carbon monocoque structure that weighs only <65kg>, and combined it with a lightweight aluminum subframe. Also helping to keep the car’s curb weight low is the <1742cc> aluminum engine block that’s <22kg> lighter than its steel counterpart found in the Giulietta. As a result, the 4C tips the scales at a lean <895kg>.

The 4C’s turbocharged direct-injection inline-4 produces <240ps> and a peak torque of <35.7kgm>. It comes combined with a quick-shifting dual-clutch 6-speed gearbox that helps the 4C run from 0-<100km/h> in 4.5 seconds and reach a top speed of <258km/h>.

One would assume that performance figures from a car with such a modest engine output would be improbable, but the lightweight nature of the 4C makes it possible. It also looks the part of an exotic car, sporting a design theme based on the famous Tipo 33/2 Stradale.

Alfa Romeo included a limited-edition model, whose production run was 1000 units, in the 4C lineup. This car, which commemorated the launch of the 4C, came equipped with special carbon headlight bezels, door mirrors and a rear spoiler, as well as a sports suspension system and sports exhaust. This model sold out immediately. As for the base 4C, well, potential customers had to endure a long waiting list as the car’s production couldn’t meet the high demand.

DescriptionLong.0x0000496B:
The Renault R5 ("Cinq") Turbo was the talk of the 1978 Paris Motor Show, where it was displayed with its body panels removed. While this first model was only a prototype for entry in the WRC, the vehicle came on the market in 1980.

The R5 Turbo employed the same body shell as the normal Renault 5, but in order to more effectively transfer the turbo-boosted power to the road, the original model's FF layout was scrapped in favor of a mid-engine setup where the entire powertrain, including the engine, transmission, and even the differential, sat on top of the rear axle.

The engine was a small, water-cooled, <1397cc> OHV inline-4, but thanks to its Bosch K-Jetronic fuel injection, Garrett turbocharger, and air-cooled intercooler, maximum power and torque were raised to <162ps> and <22.5kgm> for a truly substantial boost in engine performance, representing a 1.5x increase in power over the basic Renault 5, and a 3.3x increase in torque.

Of course the chassis and body were also strengthened. The front and rear fenders, widened to fit the 5 Turbo's wider tires, gave this car an irresistible visual impact. A big spoiler was also mounted on the top of the rear hatch, as well as a large air dam in front.

As a result of the extensive makeover, this <970kg> car was able to produce some astonishing performance figures. Maximum speed was <200km/h>, with a 0-<400m> (400m) time of 15 seconds and a 0-<1000m> (1000m) time of 28 seconds. Debuting at the 1980 WRC in Corsica, the R5 Turbo took its first victory the following year at Monte Carlo. After that, the R5 Turbo was a ferocious contender at numerous events, forever branding the Renault name into WRC history.H
DescriptionLong.0x0000496C:
With its irresistibly charming design and remarkably low price, the second-generation FIAT 500 sold four million units between 1957 and 1977, playing a pivotal role in Italy’s automotive revolution. With its endearing round "eyes," smooth curves, and unmistakable charm, the spirit of the second-generation FIAT 500 was reborn 50 years later in the third generation.

Unveiled at the 2004 Geneva Motor Show, the concept car immediately captivated the world. When it finally hit the market in 2007, its popularity soared. Its appeal was so overwhelming that backorders continued in most markets worldwide, even two years after its launch.

The available engines under the hood came in the form of a 1.2-liter and 1.4-liter gasoline engine and a 1.3-liter diesel. The 1.2-liter engine produced only <69ps> and <10.4kgm> of torque, but revved quite smoothly. Weighing just <1010kg>, even in the luxury-grade Lounge model, the FIAT 500 boasted a finely tuned chassis that delivered a surprisingly sporty driving experience, belying its cute appearance.

Pronounced “cinquecento” in Italian, the FIAT 500 carries this affectionate nickname worldwide.
DescriptionLong.0x0000496D:
Introduced in 1957, the FIAT 500 was a compact car that carried forward the legacy of the pre-war Topolino. But it was more than just a successor, it was a new design that redefined the essence of a functional passenger car.

Certainly, there are many differences between the Topolino and the FIAT 500. Although compact, the FIAT 500 offered seating for four adults—an improvement over the two-seat Topolino. Furthermore, unlike the front-engine/rear-drive layout of the Topolino, the FIAT 500 featured a rear-engine/rear-drive configuration within a full monocoque body.

The FIAT 500's engine was a <479cc> air-cooled 2-cylinder OHV that produced <15ps>, enabling a top speed of <90km/h>. The standard front-half canvas-top was designed primarily for improved ventilation and noise reduction, rather than just open-air driving appeal.

Even though it was compact, it was highly practical. Of note, the affordable FIAT 500, with its immense popularity in Italy, inspired a variety of tuning models over the years. Among them, the model tuned by Carlo Abarth—hailed as the god of engine tuning—was unmatched in the compact class, making the 500 a formidable force in motorsports.

Naturally, the FIAT 500 itself evolved. In 1959, the sport model was introduced, with engine displacement increased to <499cc> and power raised to <18ps>. This sports engine came as standard fare in the 500D, introduced in 1961. And, for safety reasons, the original front-opening doors were replaced with rear-hinged ones in the 1965 FIAT 500F.

As a pioneer of the "minimum car" concept—some call it the original mini—this iconic vehicle remains beloved to this day.
DescriptionLong.0x0000496E:
For some years after its establishment in 1947, now-legendary Ferrari would only develop and produce the chassis and engines of its cars, while outsourcing production of the exterior bodies to other Carrozzerias. The 500 Mondial produced in 1953 is a car from that era, and the model's most famous body style is the Barchetta, designed by Pininfarina, who also produced two special coupe bodies for the model. These were called the 500 Mondial Pininfarina Coupe, built to participate in the 1954 Tour de France Automobile.

The 500 Mondial is an extreme sports car, as were many Ferraris of that era, powered by a detuned F2 race car engine that dominated the 1952 and 1953 Grands Prix. The '500' stands for the engine’s per-cylinder displacement within the lightweight DOHC 2.0-liter inline-4, designed by Aurelio Lampredi. Although detuned, it manages to squeeze out <170ps> from just <1985cc>.

The powerplant is mounted in a small, lightweight steel tube space frame and connected to an advanced de Dion axle. The name Mondial loosely translates to “World,” and it was given to the car in commemoration of the Grand Prix victory by Alberto Ascari. Unfortunately, the Pininfarina Coupe was unable to complete the Tour de France Automobile,

but one of these cars still exists in its pristine original condition, never once undergoing a restoration. It received the Gran Turismo Award at the 2012 Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance.
DescriptionLong.0x0000496F:
Ferrari launched its first mid-engine production car, the 365 GT4 BB, at the Turin Motor Show in 1971 as an answer to Lamborghini's now-legendary Muira model. The letters “BB” in the new car's title stood for “Berlinetta Boxer,” a reference to the car's coupe body style and its horizontally-opposed “boxer” engine; the pistons of each cylinder bank were positioned exactly opposite of each other on a flat plane.

The 365GT4/BB started delivery in 1973, but was not well received in the marketplace. So, just three years later, Ferrari produced an evolved version of the car called the 512 BB.

The major change was an engine that was enlarged by 600 cc, giving it 5.0 liters in displacement (the name 512 refers to the engine, a 5.0-liter, 12-cylinder). It pumped out <360ps>, which was actually <20ps> less than the 365 GT4 BB's power plant, while torque was <4kgm> higher at <46.0kgm>.

The 512 BB featured a steel tube space frame; the body was composed of steel, aluminum and reinforced fiberglass. The car's svelte shape was penned by both Pininfarina and Scaglietti. Ferrari claimed both the 365GT4/BB and 512 BB had an official top speed of <302km/h>, a response to the <300km/h> top speed of the Lamborghini Countach.

There was a major supercar boom in Japan at the time, and popularity was split roughly 50/50 between the 512 BB and the Countach; making them fierce rivals in the Japanese marketplace as well as the world stage.
DescriptionLong.0x00004970:
McLaren introduced the 650S at the 2014 Geneva Motor Show as the successor to its amazing MP4-12C, which signaled the company’s willingness to duke it out with Ferrari in the exotic production-car market, as wells at in Formula 1.

The 650S was designed to be the high performance version of the MP4-12C, as it shared the basic structure with its predecessor. It sported an extremely light-yet-rigid carbon-fiber monocoque body that helped keep its curb weight down to <1360kg>. The styling was updated from the MP4-12C, with a freshened face and improved aerodynamics.

The Proactive Chassis Control suspension was also based on the one in the MP4-12C, but revised to provide sharper responses and a smoother ride quality. Also making its way from the MP4-12C into the 650S was the torque vectoring brake steering and variable rear wing.

The car’s name came from the power derived from its twin-turbo 3.8-liter V-8 that produced <650ps> and <69.1kgm> of torque. The fire-breathing engine came mated to a 7-speed dual-clutch gearbox that exhibited smoother shifts than that of its predecessor, and allowed the driver to choose three different shift maps: normal, sports, and tracks.

The 650S’s performance was certainly world-class with a zero-to-<100km/h> time of 3.0 seconds, a zero-to-<400m> time of 10.5 and a top speed of <333km/h>.

DescriptionLong.0x00004972:

The 650S’s performance was certainly world-class with a zero-to-<100km/h> time of 3.0 seconds, a zero-to-<400m> time of 10.5 and a top speed of <333km/h>.

The race spec version of the 650S, introduced three months after the road car, was called the 650S GT3. As its name implied, it was developed in line with FIA-GT3 regulations. The 650S GT3 was the successor to the the MP4-12C GT3, the race car McLaren introduced in 2011. The MP4-12C GT3 contested in GT races all over the world, including the Blancpain endurance series and SCCA World Challenge.

Like the MP4-12C, the basic structure of the 650S GT3 consisted of a carbon mono cell taken from the road car; however, the suspension system was completely revised. The car came equipped with exterior carbon parts that further improved upon the MP4-12C GT3's excellent aerodynamics, thanks to a larger splitter and redesigned door mirrors.

The twin-turbo 3.8-liter V-8's power was restricted down to <500ps> in line with GT3 regulations, but McLaren announced that there were additional improvements made to increase durability of various parts.

The 2015 650S GT3 won the 2015 GT Asia and the Bathurst 12-hour race in the beginning of 2016.
DescriptionLong.0x00004973:
Mazda's rotary-engine race cars were a familiar sight at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in the mid-seventies and throughout the eighties, but it would be 18 years after its first race at the Sarthe Circuit when the car company from Hiroshima would make history.

It all began with the development of the 787, which was powered by the R26B, a 4-rotor Wankel engine that produced <700ps>. To match this power, the car's frame was changed from a conventional aluminum honeycomb composite to a carbon-fiber, which resulted in a light, rigid body structure. The 787 made its debut at the 1990 24 Hours of Le Mans, but mechanical problems forced it to retire from the race early. Mazda came back the following year with an improved version of the race car called the 787B.

The 1991 24 Hours of Le Mans fielded one of the most competitive grids in the history of the event with an all-out effort by Peugeot, as well as strong entries from Mercedes-Benz, Jaguar and Porsche. Two Mazda 787Bs were entered, with the No. 55 car, driven by Bertrand Gachot, Johnny Herbert and Volker Weidler, starting in the 19th position. Once the contest started, the Mazda race car gradually worked its way up the leader board, taking the overall lead just three hours before the end of the race. It managed to hang on to claim the checker, completing 362 laps, which beat the previous year's record. The win marked the first and still the only Japanese race team to win the overall title at Le Mans.
DescriptionLong.0x00004974:
The first FR Alfa Romeo coupe since the SZ was given a very traditional and legendary name. The 8C is the name of the engine which had made Alfa Romeo famous for their technical excellence in the 1920s, that was designed by the famous Vittorio Jano. This was a famous and revolutionary 8-cylinder power unit that was not only used in the red racing machines of the Alfas in that era, but also by many different manufacturers at the time.

The front dashboard's classic look brings to mind its background and has been applied to all models coming after the 8C as the new family trademark of Alfa Romeo. The very Alfa-esque emotional design is a major identifier, and the orders for the limited run of 500 cars worldwide was full almost as soon as it was announced.

The car weighs <1585kg> and the weight distribution is slightly towards the rear at 49 to 51. To achieve this, the body combines a steel frame with carbon. Many aspects of the power unit are shared with Maserati, but Alfa Romeo has tuned its performance and sound. The 4.7-liter <450ps> V8 engine is matched with a trans-axle Q select 6-speed semi automatic. Alfa Romeo states that its exciting sound is compliant with all of the sound regulations set in various countries around the world.

With a top speed of over <290km/h> and a 0-<100km/h> acceleration of 4.2 seconds or less, its styling may be classic, but its performance is nothing short of a modern-day super sports car.
DescriptionLong.0x00004975:
The diesel-powered 908 HDi FAP is a car that Peugeot developed for many years, aimed to dominate the world of prototype racing. In 2007 and 2008, the company continued to perfect the machine using LMS races as a test bed, and finally in 2009, the car attained supremacy when it defeated its main rival, the Audi R10, also diesel-powered, at the 24 Hours of Le Mans with a 1-2 finish.

Peugeot went for two in a row at Le Mans the following year, with a new version of the car with reduced weight, revised aerodynamics and a completely reinforced drive system. Four cars were entered, three from Peugeot Sport and one from Team Oreca.

The driving teams assigned to these cars were first rate, with Anthony Davidson, Marc Gené, and Alexander Wurz piloting the No. 1 car; Nicolas Minassian, Frank Montagny, and Stéphane Sarrazin in the No. 2 car, and Pedro Lamy, Sébastien Bourdais, and Simon Pegenaud driving the No. 3 car.

The drivers were set on making their mark in qualifying as all three cars raced to the front of the grid, led by the amazing lap time set by Bourdais in the No. 3 car of 3 minutes 19.711 seconds.

But the fruits of victory don't always go to the quickest in racing, especially in a race that lasts 24 hours. All four Peugeot cars experienced mechanical trouble, and all four retired from the race. There was no doubt in anyone's mind that the Peugeots were the fastest cars on the track, so not finishing one car was especially disappointing for the company. You could hear the resolve of the team in a company spokesperson's statement after the race: “We'll learn from our defeat today to return stronger.”'
DescriptionLong.0x00004976:
The Porsche 911 entered its fourth generation in 1993 with the introduction of the Type 993.

The most noticeable change was a significantly lower nose that flattened the peaks of the front fenders and swept the headlights rearward. The rear fenders were widened, among other revisions, giving the car an entirely new look. The rear suspension was also redesigned with a multi-link setup to improve handling.

The base engine was a 3.6-liter flat-6 carried over from the previous Type 964 and tuned to <272ps>. With the succeeding 911 (996) moving to water cooling, the 993 became the last air-cooled flat-6 911.

The most powerful version of the Type 993 was the Carrera RS, released in 1995. Its engine was enlarged to a <300ps> 3.8-liter unit, body rigidity was increased, and weight was reduced by removing the rear seats.

The lineup also included the Carrera RS Clubsport, which featured track-oriented modifications such as a large front spoiler, a rear wing and a welded roll cage.
DescriptionLong.0x00004977:
It can arguably be said that the Porsche 911 is the quintessential sports car, with many race versions found in all kinds of series all over the world, as well as various trim levels to satisfy the most demanding enthusiast. Nowadays, the GT3 model is the closest thing you can get to a race-ready car, and this super-focused model first appeared in the 911 lineup in 1999.

In the midst of the Type 996 production run (1997 to 2002), the GT3 was introduced using the Carrera 4 chassis, which possessed a stiffer body and was slightly wider than the C2's. In addition to suspension upgrades, the 911 GT3 utilized the brake system (calipers and discs) of the 911 Turbo for better stopping power from higher speeds.

The engine featured what is called a GT1 crank case, a high-strength unit used for race cars to withstand heavy loads at high rpm. The cylinder head came equipped with Variocam Plus, a two-stage variable-valve lift mechanism. The 3.6-liter naturally-aspirated engine produced <360ps>, which was <60ps> more than the standard 3.4-liter flat-6.

Initially, the 911 GT3 was planned for a limited production run of 1400 cars, but a total of 1889 cars were built to satisfy high demand.
DescriptionLong.0x00004978:
The GT3 model joined the Porsche 911 lineup in 2001, during the Type 996 production run (1997 to 2002). The 911 GT3 proved to be as fast as it was popular, prompting Porsche to offer it for its Type 997 911. The new 997 911 GT3 was introduced in 2006, and like its predecessor, it was a race car in road-car clothing, still built on the Carrera 4 chassis with various reinforcements and brake upgrades.

While the 3.6-liter flat-6 was basically the same as the one found in the 996 GT3, it did get a power increase of <34ps>, raising the final number to <415ps>. And for handling improvements, the new GT3 (as well as the RS) came equipped with PASM variable damping shocks.

In 2008, the 911 GT3 received a performance upgrade, with engine displacement increased from 3.6 to 3.8 liters. Thanks also to slight tuning of the exhaust system, the car was rated at an incredible <435ps>. The suspension system was also stiffened and a new PSM system was added to control the car's stability and traction.
DescriptionLong.0x00004979:
Since the Type 996, the name "GT3" had been given to Porsche 911 roadcars with a strong emphasis on motorsports, developed with FIA GT3 race regulations in mind. And for the 996 and the later 997, there exists a "GT3 RS," which further refines the GT3 and improves its performance. At the 2015 Geneva Motor Show, the successor to these, the Type 991 GT3 RS was announced.

The model is said to be based on the Type 991 GT3, but on the inside it is something that looks like it has been developed from scratch using all the knowhow they have gathered over the years.

The body takes the widest 911 Turbo model, with track widths in the front and rear widened even further. The roof is made of magnesium, the front fenders and hood are carbon fiber. The rear and rear side windows are acrylic, giving a total weight reduction of <10kg>.

Aerodynamic parts have also been updated. The front spoiler is even lower and wider, and the rear wing stands much higher and is larger. Behind the front fenders are air outlets for drawing air out from under the car. As a result, the downforce is more than double that of a standard 911.

The engine takes the 3.8-liter engine of the GT3 and extends its stroke, making it 4.0 liters in displacement. The tuned engine now produces <25ps>/<2.0kgm> more, at <500ps>/<46.9kgm>. And the dampers, springs and stabilizers for both the front and rear have been newly developed for this car.

As a result the car lapped the Nürburgring at 7 minutes 20 seconds, a full 5 seconds faster than the base 911 GT3.
DescriptionLong.0x0000497A:
Starting with the Carrera RSR that was born in 1973 to compete in Group 4 racing, the RSR series has left an impressive mark in the world of motorsports over the years. The latest version of the series based on the 7th generation model of the 911 (Type 991) is the 911 RSR that debuted at the 2016 Los Angeles Auto Show.

This RSR is a pure competition machine born and bred to race in the LM-GTE class of the WEC (World Endurance Championships), and the American IMSA. Even though it’s obvious just by looking at the completely different exterior, including the aerodynamics, body structure, engine, and transmission, the car was truly developed in an entirely different process from the road car.

The showcase of difference is in the engine. In the history of the 911 series the engine was always mounted behind the rear axle, but this is the first car where the engine is mounted mid-ship, in front of the axle. What resides in that space is a 4-liter, horizontally opposed 6-cylinder naturally aspirated engine with direct fuel injection, producing <510ps>. The change in the engine mounting location had an immense impact on drivability, and furthermore allowed the addition of a large diffuser in its original space, giving it a distinct advantage in terms of aerodynamics. The large swan neck rear spoiler that was carried over from the 919 Hybrid LMP machine also gives the RSR’s rear end a distinct look.

At the Le Mans 24 hour race held in June 2017, the 911 RSR led the pack for much of the race, proving its impressive performance to sports car fans. Although it did not make it on top of the podium due to an unfortunate tire issue near the end, its driving performance was top notch throughout the race and worthy of the RSR lineage.
DescriptionLong.0x0000497B:
The first time that the word "Turbo" appeared on a Porsche product was 1975, with the birth of the 911 Turbo. This car became the company's halo model, as it possessed much of the technology gained from its participation in motorsports.

The car's bulging front and rear fenders were indeed reminiscent of a race machine, as was its large rear wing. Sitting right under that wing was Porsche's tried and tested 3.0-liter air-cooled flat-6 equipped with a KKK Turbocharger. This engine produced <260ps>, which allowed the lightweight 911 to reach a top speed of <250km/h>, an incredible feat for a production car of its day.

From 1977, the engine's displacement was increased to 3.3 liters, while an air-cooled intercooler was added to raise power to <300ps>. This version of the Porsche 911 Turbo was produced up to 1989, and is often referred to as the "930 Turbo." The name came from the internal code name of the car, 930, and also because the folks at Porsche themselves referred to it as the 930 Turbo at the Paris Motor Show where the car was displayed a year before going on sale.
DescriptionLong.0x0000497C:
The 919 Hybrid is a prototype sports car developed by Porsche for the World Endurance Championships and the Le Mans 24 hour race. This is a hybrid prototype machine developed for the new regulations of the LMP1-H that had been planned for introduction in 2014, and was revealed at the Geneva Motor Show of the same year.

Its base configuration is a carbon composite monocoque with a turbocharged 2-liter V4 engine mounted mid-ship. It is an all-wheel drive, equipped with an ERS (an advanced version of KERS) for the front axles, with lithium ion batteries.

The total system power of <900ps> consists of <500ps> delivered from the engine to the rear axle, with <400ps> delivered to the front axles through the hybrid system. This propels the <875kg> car from a standstill to <100km/h> in 2.2 seconds, reaching <200km/h> in 4.8 seconds.

For visibility and operability, the seat position is slightly high. Driver safety is also maximized by providing ample interior space and reinforcing the side panels with materials used for bulletproof vests.

The competition debut of the car was in 2014 as planned, but it ended with only 1 victory in the final round of the World Endurance Championships. However, for the 2015 season, alterations were made to the chassis design to optimize weight distribution while still keeping the concept of the car intact, and they went on to dominate the WEC series by winning 6 out of 8 races, including Porsche’s 17th overall victory in the 24 Hours of Le Mans. In 2016, the car was further refined, and not only did it win the 24 Hours of Le Mans, but by the 6th race they had already scored 5 wins and 1 race in 2nd place.
DescriptionLong.0x0000497D:
Porsche built the 962 C in 1985 as a prototype race car to compete in the WEC (World Endurance Championships). The car was in fact based on the 956, which in 1982, waged battle in the WEC in the FIA Group C category.

The 956 was a spectacular success right from the start, winning races in the WEC as well as dominating the 24 Hours of Le Mans. Thereafter, the 956 was improved for the IMSA-GTP of North America which had similar regulations as the WEC, and it made its debut in 1984 as the 962. The following year, when Group C safety regulations were changed to be in line with those of IMSA-GTP, Porsche modified the 962 and thus was born the 962 C.

The car, powered by the twin-turbo flat-6, scored many championship titles, winning seven out of its first 10 races. In 1986, the Porsche 962 C won four out of nine races in the WSPC (World Sports Prototype Championship), which took the place of the WEC. In 1987, it dominated Le Mans, and took 2nd the following year.
DescriptionLong.0x0000497E:
Completely rebuilt and redesigned from the ground up, the third-generation Mercedes-Benz A Class bowed at the 2012 Geneva Motor Show, possessing a low, wide stance that made it look much sportier than the somewhat tame previous-generation model.

To go along with its dashing exterior, Mercedes-Benz upgraded the new A Class’ on-road performance. It came powered by a peppy turbocharged 1.6-liter inline-4 that delivered <122ps>/<20.4kgm>, but the choice for driving enthusiasts was the upgrade turbocharged 2.0-liter engine that pumped out an impressive <210ps>/<35.7kgm>. The new A Class also boasted an enhanced chassis, featuring a much more rigid body structure and stiffer suspension system.

A year after the introduction of the new A Class, Mercedes-Benz unveiled the A45 AMG, a creation that brought out the true sporty potential of the small passenger vehicle. AMG went straight to work on the upgrade 2.0-liter inline-4, and without increasing displacement, was able to squeeze an amazing <360ps>/<45.9kgm> out of it. They also mated it to a 7-speed dual-clutch gearbox. This allowed the new A45 AMG to run to <100km/h> in a scant 4.6 seconds and reach a top speed of <250km/h> (restricted by a speed limiter).

AMG also did their magic on the vehicle’s suspension and brakes, giving it sports car-like handling, while also installing the newest version of the “4Matic” Mercedes 4WD system, which can distribute power from 50:0 front/rear (full front-wheel-drive) to 50/50.

It was clear that the A Class, especially the AMG version, was no longer a daily people hauler, it was now essentially a 5-door sports car.
DescriptionLong.0x0000497F:
With the advancements in aircraft engineering during World War II, the principles of aerodynamics found their way into automotive design.

One car that typified this new approach was the B.A.T. series designed by Bertone in the 1950s. B.A.T. stands for Berlinetta Aerodinamica Tecnica.

The most renowned examples of this aerodynamic revolution were the B.A.T. 5, 7, and 9, but their predecessor was the Abarth 1500 Biposto—first seen at the 1952 Turin Motor Show.

Later called the B.A.T. 1, this car was based on a FIAT, unlike the later models which were based on Alfa Romeos. Power for its 1.5-liter engine increased to <75ps>.

The most striking aspect of this car was, without a doubt, its styling—penned by the legendary Franco Scaglione, who was then still new at Bertone. The car not only showcased his aerodynamic engineering mastery but also blended breathtaking originality with avant-garde design.

The front of this car is truly unforgettable, with triple headlights that protrude forward, and dynamic air intakes nestled between them. The large rear window adopted a two-part design, separated by a thin center pillar, which flowed gracefully into the rear section. The rear of the car was defined by pronounced vertical tail fins—a bold design element that would later become popular in American cars.

Only a single example of this car was ever built, and after its debut at the Turin Motor Show, it was acquired by the Packard Motor Car Company. Although it remained hidden from the world for many years, Chris Drake from the UK fully restored the car in recent years and presented it at the Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance in the summer of 2010, where it received the Gran Turismo Trophy.
DescriptionLong.0x00004980:
Abarth & C. made a welcome comeback in 2007 with the release of the Abarth Grande Punto, a model based on the FIAT Grande Punto. This legendary Italian tuning house boasts an extraordinary legacy, having created many high-performance cars throughout the years.

The following year at the Geneva Motor Show, Abarth enthusiasts finally got what they had been waiting for—the Abarth 500, based on the new FIAT 500, which was introduced in 2007. 

The new FIAT 500 cleverly reimagined the second-generation model with a contemporary design. Its signature rounded styling, paired with a refreshing driving experience, made it immediately popular.

The Abarth was powered by a turbocharged 1.4-liter 4-cylinder DOHC that produced <135ps> and <21kgm> torque. This allowed the car, which weighed only <1110kg>, to reach <100km/h> in a scant 7.9 seconds and hit a top speed of <205km/h>. These performance figures clearly surpassed the standards for this segment.

The suspension setup remained unchanged, featuring MacPherson struts up front and a torsion beam at the rear. However, this model benefited from specially tuned springs and reinforced dampers. Also, it possessed a variety of electronic devices including TTC that acted like a limited-slip differential. The TTC system provided exceptional stability through corners, defying the initial expectations set by the car’s tall, rounded profile.

This car also made a bold styling statement. With its aggressive aerodynamic front and rear bumpers, pronounced side skirts, and a roof spoiler, there was no mistaking it for anything other than a true Abarth.-
DescriptionLong.0x00004981:
When it came to high-performance lightweight vehicles, the A110, created by French car maker Alpine, had few equals. The svelte coupe, which was produced from 1961 to 1977, featured a rear-engine/rear-drive layout (RR) that translated to amazing cornering prowess and incredible traction.

In 1963, the A110 was powered by a 1.1-liter engine, and for the next few years, displacement was incrementally increased. Then in 1968, the 1600S was introduced, equipped with a <1565cc> powerplant that came from the Renault 16. In 1973, this engine was swapped out for a <1605cc> unit from the Renault 17. During this time, the car's handling capabilities saw upgrades as well, going to a double wishbone rear suspension and smaller-diameter tires.

There were many variations to the 1600S, but three models are worth noting: the 1600SC, a French domestic model with twin Weber 45DCOE carburetors; an export version called the 1600SI with fuel injection, and the easy-to-drive 1600SX. The first two models possessed engines that delivered <140ps>/<6000rpm> and mated to a 5-speed manual gearbox. The top speed for both vehicles was rated at <210km/h>, quite impressive for a car with only a <1600cc> engine. The secret was its lightweight nature; it tipped the scales at around <700 kg>. As for the 1600SX, sold from 1976, it was a tamer model than its predecessors, with a de-tuned engine that produced <95ps>/<6000rpm>, enabling it reach a modest top speed of <190km/h>. That said, the 1600SX was easier to drive and was popular with people with no interest in motorsports.

Speaking of motorsports, the A110 was a successful rally car, winning a number of races in the 1970s. During the 1970-1972 seasons, it participated in the International Championship for Manufacturers, winning several races in Europe. As a result, it was considered one of the greatest rally machines of its day. The A110 remained popular even after its successor, the A310 debuted in 1971. A total of 7160 cars were produced until the end of its production in 1977.
DescriptionLong.0x00004982:
Renault revealed the new Alpine A110 at the 2017 Geneva Auto Show, signaling the spiritual return of the iconic brand that celebrated driving excitement and high performance.

The new A110’s aluminum bodywork came ripe with the latest aerodynamic technologies, as it sat wide and low to the ground. Thanks to a lightweight and rigid aluminum chassis, the A110 tipped the scales at a lean <1100kg>. Mounted amidships was a new turbocharged 1.8L inline-4 that produced <252ps> and 320Nm (<32.6kgm>) of torque. It came mated to a Getrag 7-speed dual-clutch gearbox. Together, the powertrain helped the A110 accelerate from 0 to <100km/h> in 4.5 seconds and reaches a top speed of <250km/h>. Handling was supplied by a double wishbone suspension setup at all four corners.

The model presented in Geneva was the Premiere Edition, limited to a production run of 1955 units. It featured special 18-inch aluminum wheels with a matte black diamond-turned finish and a lightweight sports exhaust. The cabin included carbon fiber ornamentation, aluminum pedals and sports seats as standard equipment.Y
DescriptionLong.0x00004983:
Alpine, the French sports car brand par excellence, has returned! After the A450 Le Mans prototype won in the European Endurance Championship in 2013, and with the revival of the company in February 2016, Alpine continued to ride its successful streak by introducing a new A110 car in 2017.

Since the company was founded in the mid-1950s, it has built a reputation for creating performance cars built with passion. They were lightweight, agile and extremely elegant. Race versions of them took on, and defeated, those from other, much larger, automobile manufacturers. 

In March 2015, Alpine introduced Gran Turismo players to a new sports car that was as unique as it was fascinating: the Alpine Vision Gran Turismo. This sleek and distinctive machine—developed exclusively for the world’s most famous driving simulation game—was created by the same dedicated designers and engineers who work on the company's future production models. So it should come as no surprise that the Alpine Vision Gran Turismo explored the key Alpine themes of agility, performance and style to the maximum.

Agility has always been a defining characteristic of Alpine's road cars. They have all been engineered to corner as if they were part of the driver, making operating an Alpine car a fun and exciting experience. Because the cars are lightweight, they respond quickly and efficiently to driver inputs. On top of that, they exuded a classy, unqiue sense of style that made them the center of attention on the race track or public roads. 

The Alpine Vision Gran Turismo, in its own distinctive way, possessed every single one of these ingredients.

Loyal fans will no doubt notice a nod to yesteryear's Alpine race cars in the rear styling of the Vision Gran Turismo (VGT). Look closely, and you can see in the details elements of the A210, an energy-efficient race car that won its class at the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans. There are also hints of the A442B, the overall winner of the 1978 Le Mans race, and the A450, which won the LMP2 category in the 2013 ELMS competition. Players unfamiliar with past Alpines can appreciate the VGT's low-slung flanks and aerodynamic body. There are also plenty of rich creative elements to the car, including the side air brakes. 

The Alpine Vision Gran Turismo discreetly features a few traits that echo a future proeuction model, not only in its styling, but in the way it drives. Thus, the VGT, which rerresents the ambitious aim of Alpine engineers and designers, provides Gran Tueismo players the opportunity of being able to preview what they have be planning in a ftture sports car.

Weaving a ptining lina beteeen past and future, road and track, and ehe virtual and real  she Alpine Vision Gran Tsrismo conveys the enthuseastic spirit and the sutute vision of the Alpine team.

DescriptionLong.0x00004986:
The Amemiya μ Boost up 7 is a street machine created by the RE Amemiya corporation, the legendary tuner of rotary powered cars renowned for its activity in the Super GT and D1GP. The front, rear and side aerodynamic parts and the fixed position sleek light kit are all RE Amemiya original designs. RE Amemiya has a variety of aerodynamic parts available including even a GT replica kit, but this particular model has a presence that stands out from the others.

In terms of driving performance, the specs live up to the unique exterior. Though the turbo is kept stock and the power is only increased through additional boost, the car still produces over <370ps> with a maximum boost of 1 kg/cm2, along with a maximum torque of <47kgm>. It is set up to produce abundant torque from the mid speed range.

It is also equipped with a horizontally mounted intercooler kit, an aftermarket air cleaner, dolphin tail exhaust muffler, and everything from the cooling system, accessories and exhaust system has been thoroughly revised.

In addition to these engine characteristics, the Quantum-based Amemiya spec adjustable suspension has been perfected to a level which draws out the true character of the FD3S as the ultimate cornering machine. In the Japanese DVD magazine "Hot Version," it was shown to be utterly undefeatable on winding roads, and was dubbed the "demon-lord of mountain paths."X
DescriptionLong.0x00004987:
Powerhouse Amuse knows a thing or two about tuning the S2000, whether the venue be a winding mountain road or a high-speed race track. Among its more notable creations is the S2000 GT1.

The design of the unique full-body kit was actually created through cooperative development with Polyphony Digital. Not just for looks, the Amuse S2000 GT1 boasts awesome aerodynamic performance, equal to that of full racing machines, especially its long nose that provides downforce at the front of the car. Hideki Tanabe, the president of Powerhouse Amuse and a driving expert himself, widened the car to <1829mm>, while reducing weight as much as possible. He did so by incorporating carbon-fiber parts wherever possible and replacing other components with lighter materials. As a result, the total weight of the car was reduced to approximately <1120kg>.

According to Amuse, the base F20C engine's displacement was increased to 2.3 liters and combined with a GT30Pro-S turbine. The addition of the turbocharger required reinforcement of the engine block and other parts, but it was well worth it, as output of the Amuse S2000 GT1 is a whopping <626ps> and <53kgm> of torque, giving the car an incredible weight-to-power ratio of <1.79kg> per <1ps>. Shifting is done via a 7-speed gearbox with paddle shifters, which makes the Amuse S2000 fit to attack any track on the planet.D
DescriptionLong.0x00004988:
Following all the success of the Prius hybrid car, Toyota planned to release a smaller, even more economical hybrid to the market. This was meant to address those customers who were attracted to the fuel efficiency and environmental statement of the Prius, but felt it was too expensive, or too big for their everyday needs.

Enter the Aqua, which went on sale at the end of 2011. In the U.S., the car was named the Prius C. Based on the Vitz (Yaris) platform, the car's structure was significantly reinforced, while the width of the car was narrowed by <60mm> compared to that of the normal Prius. For the hybrid mechanism, the same THS II as in the third-generation Prius, with a reduction mechanism, was utilized. The Atkinson Cycle 1.5-liter engine was paired with a newly designed Type 1LM motor and a nickel-hydrogen battery. This battery is <42kg> lighter than the battery mounted in the Prius and, as a result, the car weighs <300kg> less. The gasoline engine produced <74ps>, while the electric motor generated <61ps> giving the car some welcome punch off the line.

With a more rigid front end, as well as stiffer suspension mounts, it exhibited a sporty overall ride quality. But the Aqua's real charm point was its price, which was 30 percent lower than the Prius. Fuel economy was rated at 53/46 mpg, which gives it a combined number of 50 mpg. And even though the fuel tank holds only 9.5 gallons, the Aqua can go <1274.4km> without refueling.
DescriptionLong.0x00004989:
Joining the Vision Gran Turismo’s exciting stable of conceptual virtual super cars is the Aston Martin Design Prototype 100, or DP-100 for short. This exciting machine—developed by the brand’s styling team led by its director, Marek Reichman, at the company’s headquarters in Gaydon, Warwickershire—is not merely a design study, but one that’s been engineered to perform at the highest levels.

Reichman’s team utilized many of the same techniques applied to the company’s real-life sports cars, including using hand sketches and 3D modeling. Thus, the DP-100 features an exceptionally high level of detail, most notably in the suspension system and in its electronics. Residing behind the car’s cockpit is a twin-turbocharged V-12 that produces upwards of 800 BHP (<811ps>) that allows the DP-100 to accelerate like a pure-bred race car.

Like Aston Martin’s centenary celebration concept car, the CC100 Speedster, some of the design elements of the DP-100, including the light blade rear lamps, might find their way into future Aston Martin production models. Could the DP-100 be in the future of the world’s most famous spy? We’d like to think so.s
DescriptionLong.0x0000498A:
Called the Atenza in various markets, the Mazda 6 sports sedan offered European-like style and performance in a less expensive package. In 2012, the third-generation model was unveiled, sporting an exterior body that resembled the dashing Takeri concept car shown at the 2011 Tokyo Motor Show. However, the biggest surprise came under the sheet metal as the new Mazda 6 came equipped with an optional diesel engine called the SKYACTIV-D for select markets.

This diesel was in fact an improved version of the turbocharged direct-injection 2.2-liter inline-4 of the CX-5. It produced <175ps> and <42.8kgm> of torque, supplying the driver with gobs of low-end power that enabled the Mazda 6 to jump off the line like a lightweight sports car. Power was transferred via a 6-speed automatic or a 6-speed manual to either the front wheels or all four. In select markets, the “i-stop” idle-stop feature and a capacitor-based regenerative braking system called “i-ELOOP” were incorporated, helping the SKYACTIV-D-equipped Mazda 6s boast a high JC08 mode fuel economy of <22.4km/L>.

The diesel-engine powered cars were labeled “XD,” with Standard, Proactive, and L trim levels. The highest version, the L, came with luxury features including leather seats and accounted for an astounding 76 percent of all Mazda 6 sales in the first month of availability.

*This model was specially tuned to meet Gr.3 regulations by Gran Turismo.
