DescriptionLong.0x0000498E:
Toyota's weapon of choice for the GT500 class of the Super GT Series from 2014 to 2016 was the race version of the Lexus RC F production car, which was released in October 2014.

Because of new regulations from 2014, the car underwent a several changes to conform to the new rules. The weight and rigidity of the monocoque and center of gravity were altered, while new dampers, brakes and a rear wing were added, making it look like a true DTM machine. Powering the car was a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4 with direct injection (called the RI4AG), which also saw use in Super Formula cars. Because of of a new regulation that limited fuel flow from <100kg/h> to <95kg/h>, improvements were made elsewhere so the car could produce more power with less fuel.

The 2016 model was the final version of this RC F race car, with the au TOM’S RC F wearing the ace car number 36. It placed 3rd in the third race of the season and 2nd in Round 6, ultimately finishing 5th overall out of 15 cars.
DescriptionLong.0x0000498F:
Audi has jumped into the EV fray with a purely electric-powered race car for the future. Called the Audi e-tron Vision Gran Turismo, this awesome machine was initially developed to be a virtual model in the "Vision Gran Turismo" lineup; however, Audi felt it was just too good to keep it exclusively digitized, so it built a running prototype that was used as a race taxi in the Formula E racing series. This makes the e-tron Vision Gran Turismo the first virtual concept car in the Vision Gran Turismo series that became a real-life fully functioning car.

The new race car is reminiscent of the Audi 90 IMSA GTO, which thrilled fans in the North American IMSA GTO racing series in 1989 with drivers such as Hans-Joachim Stuck, Walter Röhrl, Hurley Haywood and Scott Goodyear. The car was far ahead of its time, thanks to its combination of lightweight construction, a powerful turbocharged inline-5 engine, and quattro all-wheel-drive.

The Audi e-tron Vision Gran Turismo, which fans will be able to experience virtually starting April 2018, is powered by three 200 kW (<272ps>) electric motors: two motors for the rear axle and one at the front. Total output is a whopping 600 kW (<815ps>), and when combined with its lean curb weight of <1450kg>, the result is a weight-to-power ratio of <1.78kg> per horsepower. The Audi is also corners with the best of them, thanks in part to a 50/50 front/rear weight distribution and all-wheel-drive with variable power distribution. And just like the company's Formula E race cars, the Audi e-tron Vision Gran Turismo has only one forward gear.
DescriptionLong.0x00004990:
The Audi Vision Gran Turismo, developed by Audi Design exclusively for the "Vision Gran Turismo" competition and launched on the 15th anniversary of the series, came in both hybrid and fully-electric versions. Launched on the 15th anniversary of Gran Turismo, these exciting race machines offer a look into the future of motorsports.

The hybrid Audi Vision Gran Turismo is equipped with e-tron quattro, making it all-wheel-drive. It borrows the same technology as the 2012 Le Mans-winning race car, which featured motor-driven front wheels and a conventional rear-wheel setup. The front wheels of the Audi Vision Gran Turismo is powered by a 400 kW (<544ps>) motor (MGU-K) that recovers energy when braking. The rear tires are powered by a turbocharged 3.4-liter V-6 that produces 550 kW (<748ps>), making total output an impressive 950 kW (<1292ps>), which is more than many of today's LMP1 hybrid racers. It comes mated to a sequential 7-speed gearbox actuated by paddles on the steering wheel. The weight-to-power ratio for the Audi Vision Gran Turismo is less than one kilogram per horsepower.

The new race car is reminiscent of the Audi 90 IMSA GTO, which thrilled fans in the North American IMSA GTO racing series in 1989 with drivers such as Hans-Joachim Stuck, Walter Röhrl, Hurley Haywood and Scott Goodyear. The car was far ahead of its time, thanks to its combination of lightweight construction, a powerful turbocharged inline-5 engine, and quattro all-wheel-drive.

You can tell the all-electric version from the hybrid by the wheels: the former comes with 18-inchers all around, while the hybrid race car has 20-inch wheels in front with 21-inch examples at the rear.=
DescriptionLong.0x00004991:
The Lamborghini Aventador LP 750-4 Superveloce, introduced in 2015, was the most potent road car from the manufacturer to date (only to be eclipsed by the Aventador S a year later). True to its name of Superveloce, which was first used on the legendary Miura, this car was indeed "super fast."

It came powered by a 6.5-liter naturally-aspirated V-12 that produced <50ps> more power than the standard Aventador with <750ps> on tap, sending the power to all four wheels via a 7-speed semiautomatic transmission. The performance numbers of this mid-engine exotic were staggering, as it recorded a 0-<100km/h> time of 2.8 seconds, reached <200km/h> in just 8.6, and accelerated to <300km/h> in 24.9 seconds. The top speed of the car was estimated at more than <350km/h>. When it was time to slow down, the Aventador's excellent braking system needed only <30m> of tarmac to bring the car to a halt from <100km/h>.

Only 600 coupe models were produced, but a convertible version was introduced later with a limited production run of 500 units.
DescriptionLong.0x00004992:
The Murciélago, which had been a descendant of the Countach, had been the flagship of Lamborghini for nearly 10 years since its debut in 2001, and the time had come for a successor. The company introduced that successor at the 2011 Geneva Motor Show when it unveiled the Aventador.

The newest bull in the stable inherited the scissor doors of its predecessors, as well as a wind-cutting wedge profile that characterized nearly every Lamborghini model ever. While it retained much of the visual cues of the Murciélago, under the sheet metal, things had been completely changed. The steel tube space frame of the Murciélago was replaced with a carbon monocoque and forward/rear aluminum subframes, with nearly every single body part composed of carbon fiber or aluminum. As a result, the new car weighed roughly <100kg> less than the Murciélago, tipping the scales at <1575kg>.

Mounted amidships was a 6.5-liter, DOHC 48 valve V12 that produced <700ps> at <8250rpm> and <70.4kgm> of torque at <5500rpm>. The power was transferred to the ground via an electronically-controlled forward/aft torque-splitting mechanism and a single clutch 7-speed semi-automatic gearbox that shifted 40 percent faster than the e-Gear on the Gallardo.

The pushrod-type double-wishbone suspension system, often used in racing, was the first of its kind in a production car. Thanks to all of its cutting-edge technology, the Aventador reached a top speed of <350km/h>, which was <8km/h> faster than the the Murciélago. It ran the 0-<100km/h> in 2.9 seconds, 0.3 seconds quicker than its predecessor.

In an era where car makers concentrated on efficiency and environmental friendliness, leave it to Lamborghini to throw all that out the window and bring us a car that truly rocked our world.
DescriptionLong.0x00004993:
The Beat defied every kei-car convention and was an instant "classic in the making" for Honda. Not only was it a convertible — a very rare attribute for kei cars — it had a mid-engine layout, making the Beat totally unique.

The little Honda measured <3295mm> from bumper to bumper, sat <1395mm> wide and <1175mm> tall. What's especially notable is the Beat's curb weight of only <760kg>. The mass was distributed front and rear just like a large exotic car, with 43 percent of its weight over the front wheels and 53 over rear. The engine, which was situated immediately behind the cabin, was a <656cc> naturally-aspirated inline-3 that produced <64ps>. Despite being classified as a kei engine, it was quite high-tech, featuring a multi-joint throttle and an engine control system that trickled down from the company’s Formula 1 program. A 5-speed manual gearbox managed the power sent to the rear wheels.

The Beat's handling was in a league of its own. The suspension was tuned for sporty driving, and Honda incorporated different size wheels for the front (13 in.) and rear (14 in.). The brakes were excellent, being fitted with discs at all four corners, the first for a kei car.

Despite the somewhat pricey nature of the Beat, Honda ended up selling 33,672 of this svelte convertible until production was halted in 1996.
DescriptionLong.0x00004994:
The Beetle is an important part of Volkswagen’s history and heritage. But beneath its charming exterior lies a rich motorsport pedigree. It enjoyed its moment in the racing spotlight as far back as the 1950s. Early in its storied history, the Beetle won the East African Safari Rally three times and held its own in the Acropolis Rally in Greece. The reborn Beetle, which debuted in 1998, even inspired its own one-make racing series. In more recent years, it achieved notable success in the Global Rallycross in the U.S.

This Beetle Gr.3 is a model that traces this racing legacy of the Beetle. Its extensively reworked exterior and internals embody the spirit of racing success that Volkswagen has achieved over decades of competition.

The body has been widened to accommodate larger-diameter wheels, while the roofline has been lowered to reduce frontal area, resulting in a silhouette reminiscent of a classic chop-top Beetle. The aggressive front spoiler, functional air outlets channeling flow from the front tires to the door panels, and the towering rear wing all speak volumes about this car’s performance pedigree.

At its heart lies a DOHC 2.0-liter inline-4 paired with a high-pressure turbocharger, mated to VW's proven 7-speed DSG transmission. While output is adjusted according to Balance of Performance (BoP) regulations for each race, rest assured, it packs more than enough punch to compete fiercely in the Gr.3 category.

This racing Beetle exists in an entirely different realm from the charming, street-going Beetles you might be familiar with.
DescriptionLong.0x00004995:
Following in the tradition of successful BMW touring cars of the 1970s, the BMW design team has created an uncompromising road racer for the modern era.

Crisp proportions and a dynamic silhouette give the BMW Vision Gran Turismo the appearance that it's in constant motion, even when standing still. Front and rear spoilers provide optimum downforce, while the various carbon fiber pieces found throughout the car's body have been designed to reduce drag and keep curb weight at a minimum. The car tips the scales at a lean <1180kg>, with the weight distributed 50:50, front and rear.

Under the hood is a powerful twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-6 that delivers a maximum power of 404 kW/<549ps> between <6200rpm> and <7300rpm>. Peak torque comes at 680 Nm/<69kgm> at a low <1900rpm>. A sequential 6-speed transmission, operated by gearshift paddles on the steering wheel, distributes engine power to the driven rear axle.

The car's M paint scheme pays homage to the company's past successes in touring-car racing, while the bold styling language points to what may lie ahead.
DescriptionLong.0x00004996:
As the sports-car market waned globally, Toyota and Subaru decided that the world needed to be reminded of how much fun driving a sports car could be. So they joined forces and produced a front-engine/rear-drive two-door machine with a sleek body style and plenty of attitude. Toyota called its version the 86, while the Subaru went by the name BRZ.

The cars had slightly different visual cues both inside and out, but it was still obvious that they were essentially the same product. If anything, the BRZ felt slightly more upscale, designed to attract a slightly more mature buyer. Its name stood for Boxer (engine), Rear-wheel drive, and Zenith.

The BRZ fit the driver like a glove, with an overall length of <4240mm>, width of <1775mm>, and riding on a <2570mm> wheelbase. Under the hood was the company's 2.0-liter horizontally-opposed 4-cylinder engine that boasted an extremely low center of gravity. It came equipped with Toyota’s D-4S fuel injection technology that helped it produce an impressive <200ps>. While the engine provided plenty of pop, it was the car's handling that made it special, thanks in part to a rigid body structure and sport-tuned suspension system that consisted of struts up front and a double-wishbone setup at the rear.

After making its debut in 2012, Subaru refined the BRZ every year. In 2015, the car received a revised power-steering system and extra rigidity, making this jewel feel sharper through corners and even more fun to drive.
DescriptionLong.0x00004997:
Bugatti Vision Gran Turismo is a project as realistic as possible for Bugatti fans to introduce a thoroughbred Bugatti to the virtual world. The result is a symbiosis of technology, tradition and aesthetics, where every design feature has an actual purpose.

The Bugatti designers drew their inspiration from the brand's racing tradition. Bugatti enjoyed great success in racing in the 1920s and 1930s. Historical inspiration for the modern virtual race car came, in particular, from the Bugatti Type 57 Tank and its victories in the 24 Hours of Le Mans races in 1937 and 1939.

The design of the Vision Gran Turismo shows at first glance that Bugatti DNA meets cutting-edge racing technology. Marked by large convex surfaces in contrast with concave transitions and strong lines, the proportions of the vehicle are uncompromisingly athletic and designed for maximum performance. The designers have unmistakably integrated key features of the Bugatti design DNA into the virtual race car's design with every vehicle component having a real performance function. The horseshoe on the front grille acts as a support for the front splitter. The center fin, which derives from the legendary Type 57 SC Atlantic, makes an important contribution to the car's dynamic stability and accommodates the kinematic system for the rear wing, which controls the air brake and the drag reduction system (DRS). The architecture of the interior continues the clean lines of the exterior. Every aspect of the interior is geared to racing.

The virtual race car was developed in close collaboration with the Bugatti engineers and is based on modern racing technology and aerodynamic analyses. To attain the performance goals, the Bugatti Vision Gran Turismo is driven by a W16 engine, which delivers the engine power of 1230 kW (<1650 BHP>) and 1580 Nm (161.1 kgfm) to all four wheels. The engineers have calculated that the Bugatti Vision Gran Turismo can drive at over 400 km/h (250 mph) on four sections of the virtual Le Mans track reaching an overall max speed of 447.59 km/h (278 mph). 

The Bugatti Vision Gran Turismo is the ultimate race car, and at the same time a true Bugatti.

*This model was specially tuned to meet Gr.1 regulations by Gran Turismo.
DescriptionLong.0x00004999:
The 6th generation model of the Chevy Camaro, America’s legendary sports car, was revealed in the spring of 2015.

The styling followed in the retro-modern design that was highly popular in the market in the last generation. However, the inside of the car received a full makeover. The platform was changed from the "Zeta" platform of the previous model to the "Alpha" platform shared with cars like the Cadillac CTS, but with roughly 70% of its parts developed specifically for the Camaro.

The body utilizes aluminum in various parts, improving the rigidity of the body by 28% and reducing the weight by over <90kg>. The suspension mounted on this body was also newly designed, with a multi-link MacPherson strut in the front and a 5 link suspension in the rear.

The biggest news regarding the engine was that a turbocharged 2-liter inline-4 producing <279ps> of power and <40.8kgm> of torque was added to the lineup. Improvements were also made to the existing 3.6-liter V6, raising both power and torque slightly to <340ps> and <39.3kgm> respectively. In addition, an LT1 6.2-liter V8, the same engine as in the Corvette, is also available in the lineup, producing <461ps> of power and <62.9kgm> of torque.

The sports grade model powered by this LT1 is the "SS." It is equipped with 20 inch wheels and Brembo brakes, and in the case of manual transmission models, it comes equipped with active rev matching as well as an optional magnet ride control suspension.=
DescriptionLong.0x0000499A:
The Ford Mustang was a hit compact sports car that took the world by storm. The success of the Mustang was due to its excellent performance, low price, and a effective marketing campaign, so naturally, Ford's main rival, General Motors, was quick to produce a rival. That came in the form of the Chevrolet Camaro that appeared in 1966.

While the Camaro was launched to a plenty of high praise, it could not quite eclipse the sales numbers of the Mustang. So, Chevy decided to up the ante and introduce an even higher-performance version of the car, which it called the Z28. The 302-cu.-in. displacement (5.0 liters) was set to meet the regulations for the Trans-Am racing series. While it did well on the race track, it performed well at dealerships. Chevrolet saw sales of the Camaro increase, thanks to a new halo model that did wonders to the car's image.

The 1969 model is the most popular out of all the Camaros, and the Z28 is the most coveted model, for it truly represents the golden era of American pony cars.
DescriptionLong.0x0000499B:
The sixth-generation Chevrolet Camaro was largely an evolution of the previous model, which effectively combined elements of the original car with modern-day design cues. While its dimensions remained relatively unchanged, the new model weighed in approximately <100kg> lighter, making it quicker and more agile than ever before.

The most powerful model in the 2018 Camaro lineup was the ZL1, which came equipped with the LT4 engine, a 5.7-liter V8 lifted from the Corvette Z06. It produced <659ps> and <89.8kgm> of torque, allowing the pony car to run from 0 to <100km/h> in 3.5 seconds and reach a top speed of <318km/h>.

Chevrolet also offered the “1LE” performance package (as it had since the third-generation model), which gave the car even higher performance. For the 2018 model, this package included a large deflector, a rear wing, a diffuser, a dedicated suspension system, and specially developed tires. The 2018 Camaro Z1 with the 1LE package lapped the Nürburgring in 7 minutes 16.04 seconds, greatly surpassing the performance of your average supercar.
DescriptionLong.0x0000499C:
As the most popular form of motorsports in Japan, the All Japan Grand Touring Championship (JGTC) featured the country's top car makers doing battle on the country's most famous racetracks. The series was renamed the Super GT Series in 2005, with races held in Malaysia and China, expanding its appeal throughout Asia. So it was understandable that Japanese automobile manufacturers poured plenty of energy and resources into producing results in this racing series.

Toyota was among the early pioneers, whose Supra, running in the GT500 class, was the main challenger to the Nissan GT-R that had dominated the series for three straight years beginning with the first year of the championship in 1993. In 1997, the Supra finally dethroned the GT-R and became series champion with the number 36 Castrol Tom's Supra.

The winning car was piloted by Michael Krumm and Pedro de la Rosa, who began racing the Tom's Supra starting with the second round of that year. In their next five races, they won two races and placed 2nd and 3rd in two others to secure the championship. This was accomplished despite the fact that the car had not changed greatly from the previous year; the only differences were a switch from an "H"-pattern gearbox to a Hewland 6-speed sequential transmission, and lowering engine displacement to 2.0 liters to decrease weight. Still, the 3S-GT engine produced nearly <500ps>.

When all this was combined with better structural rigidity, an improved suspension system and better aerodynamics, the GT500 race Supra had no equals.
DescriptionLong.0x0000499D:
Throughout the modern racing era, Porsche has traditionally used the 911 to participate in major sports-car races, but in 2015, they surprised many by turning to the Cayman as its entry in GT4 races

The Cayman GT4 was the fastest Cayman ever, with many components carried over from the 911. It came with a 3.8-liter flat-6 from the 911 Carrera S that produced more power than the 911 Carrera at <385ps>. The front suspension and brakes were lifted from the 911 GT3, which meant it handled amazingly well and had plenty of stopping power.

The following year, the GT4 was even further refined, creating the Cayman GT4 Clubsport. This special Cayman was a pure race version designed exclusively for the race track. Any and all creature comforts on the road-going model were deleted to make it as lightweight as possible.

A roll cage protected the driver, and the seats were replaced with full bucket types. It also came with a DCT gearbox and the suspension and brakes used components equal to that of the 911 GT3 Cup car. While the engine was left as is, the mid-engine GT4 Clubsport was the ultimate Cayman and is sure to go down in the annals of Porsche history.
DescriptionLong.0x0000499E:
The first-generation Dodge Challenger debuted in 1970 as a sister car to the Plymouth Barracuda, using the same E-body.

In the mid-1960s, the U.S. featured a variety of popular pony cars (cheap, high-performance and stylish cars), such as the Ford Mustang, Chevrolet Camaro and Pontiac Firebird. The Challenger came at the tail end of this boom.

Despite being a little late to the party, the car was welcomed with open arms by the public, thanks to its attractive styling that was characterized by a flowing silhouette and smooth lines. Designed by Carl Cameron, who had designed the 1966 Charger, the car would retain much of its visual character when the third-generation model would be released 40 years later at the 2006 North American International Auto Show.

The original Challenger came in three trim levels: The 6, the Challenger V8, and Challenger R/T (Road/Track), in both hardtop and convertible versions. In addition, there was the T/A that served as a homologation model for a SCCA Trans-Am race car.E
DescriptionLong.0x0000499F:
The 2J may well be the most innovative, wildest racing machine ever created. The car, characterized by its big boxy rear end, entered the 1970 SCCA Can-Am racing series in North America, as the first machine in the series to feature active ground effects... in the form of a giant vacuum.

The Can-Am series was quite unusual as, at the time, there was no rule to limit the amount of horsepower for its race cars. Chaparral boss, Texas oil magnate Jim Hall, pulled a wild card from his sleeve when he created a race car that utilized two engines: one was a <700 ps> powerplant to power the car and the other, an air-cooled snowmobile engine that powered a pair of large fans to suck the air flowing underneath the car, thus making it “stick” to the road surface. The area between the sides of the bodywork and the ground were sealed by floating pieces of high-strength Lexan. Nicknamed “The Vacuum Cleaner,” the Chaparral 2J astounded race fans and the other Can-Am drivers alike.

Aside from its odd looks, the 2J often took pole position by several seconds over heady competition that included the previously-dominant McLaren M8D...that is, when it was running. The 2J experienced many mechanical problems in its maiden season, making every race it entered a thrilling event.

Before the start of the 1971 season, the SCCA banned the use of engines used for purposes other than powering the car itself, and the Chaparral 2J was banished from motorsports forever.
DescriptionLong.0x000049A0:
Conceived as a "Garage 56" Le Mans Experimental Prototype, the Chevrolet Chaparral 2X Vision Gran Turismo is a look into the future of motorsports and inspired by the combined sensations of flying in a wing suit and a Moto GP race bike... an experience where the 2X pilot flies around the circuit, headlong, just inches from the race surface. The 2X’s Chevrolet power unit is unlike anything seen on the track before... it literally thrusts itself down the track with laser pulse shock waves generated by an advanced propulsion system from Chevrolet.

The driving position creates one of the most immersive and exciting experiences ever imagined in four wheel motorsports. The vehicle architecture and design take its shape as a result of the "forward flight" driving position, one where the pilot becomes at one with the structure of the car. Once on board, with the canopy retracted to the closed position, the 2X forms a totally unique envelope around the pilot’s outstretched body. Hand and foot controls operate independently and involve all of the frictionless, magnetic bearing wheels. Vehicle acceleration, deceleration and direction is controlled by the movement & physical inputs of the 2X pilot, a true application of four points of control. Braking is handled by a combination of Brembo magnetic re-gen calipers and deployable AeroBrake panels in the 2X bodywork.

The integral BodyFrame is created using a unique "layup schedule" which allows the entire structure to act in unison with the 2X suspension. The main body also incorporates the super-ridged propulsion structure which ensures absolute accuracy of the thrust parabola to the laser pulse cone. The variable positioning of the thrust cone vanes serve to create propulsion and downforce by the simultaneous use of this multi-vane adjustability and a lower Thrust Vectoring panel. The combination of these two technologies allows the Chaparral 2X pilot to fine tune downforce to the exact spot on a given circuit, actually "pressing" the tire’s contact patch onto the track surface and enhancing mechanical grip where needed most.

The Chevrolet Chaparral 2X Vision Gran Turismo. The spirit of Jim Hall’s amazing legacy of motorsport innovation embodied in a bold statement. One which will revolutionize the future of Le Mans Experimental prototypes. Like nothing you’ve ewer seen or heard before.M
DescriptionLong.0x000049A1:
The Dodge Charger has always stood for brute force in the passenger-car segment, ever since the car made its original debut in 1966. Since then, the Charger has been reborn as a 4-door sedan, but with still the same in-your-face brashness of past cars. One particular trim offered an even greater dose of attitude: the Dodge Charger SRT Hellcat.

Back in 2005, the third-generation Charger made its debut after nearly a 20-year absence. Chrysler reintroduced the brand to an eager public, arming the top-of-the-line version with a “Hemi” engine as an ode to powerful Chryslers of the past. The modern-day Charger’s Hemi came in the form of a <477ps> 6.4-liter V8.

Sure, that’s a lot of power to some, but not to the engineers at SRT, the high-performance division of Chrysler. In 2014, they supercharged the Hemi, making it into a fire-breathing monster that pumped out a whopping <717ps> and <81.6kgm> of asphalt-crinkling torque. With a reinforced 8-speed automatic transmission, the new car, called the Charger SRT Hellcat, accelerated to 60 mph in an amazing 3.7 seconds and registered a top speed of <328.3km/h>.

While the Charger SRT Hellcat’s innards were basically the same as those of the 2-door Dodge Challenger SRT Hellcat, the sedan version was actually 0.2 seconds faster in the quarter-mile, at 11.0 seconds flat. What’s even more impressive was that this super sedan, which was arguably the fastest 4-door in the world in its day, came at the reasonable price of $63,995.a
DescriptionLong.0x000049A2:
Unveiled in 2014, the Charger SRT Hellcat is the most powerful production model of the long-running Dodge Charger series, which was first released in 1966.

The third rendition of the Charger was introduced in 2005 as a high-performance sports sedan, but the Hellcat was a different animal altogether. With a 6.2-liter Hemi engine meticulously tuned by SRT — Chrysler's high-performance development team. By adding a supercharger, output was increased to an astounding <717ps> with <81.6kgm> maximum torque. Coupled to a reinforced 8-speed automatic transmission, the car ran from zero to 60 mph in 3.7 seconds and reached a top speed of <328.3km/h>.

While the car's drivetrain was identical to the Challenger Hellcat, the Charger Hellcat could reach the quarter-mile mark a bit quicker at 11 seconds second flat, 0.2 seconds faster than its stablemate. The version of the Charger Hellcat you see here is an original model created by Gran Turismo.

*This safety car version is an original model created by Gran Turismo.
DescriptionLong.0x000049A3:
The SEMA show is the world's largest annual custom car show hosted in Las Vegas, Nevada of the U.S every fall. At SEMA every year, Gran Turismo picks out cars that fits the philosophy of Gran Turismo for the "GT Awards". The car that won "Best of Show" in the Gran Turismo Awards of 2013 was this 1967 Chevrolet Nova.

The original Nova is a popular small car of Chevrolet built between the 1960s and 1970s. While there were high performance top grade models powered by V8 engines, at the base is a simple, functional car that was made as a daily driver for youths and families.

The shop who turned this modest family car into a crazy hotrod is Chris Holstrom Concepts, a specialty shop from Washington state. Chris Holstrom stripped the Nova down and started integrating high performance parts to create this Monster Nova.

Under the hood is the LS9, a supercharged 6.2L engine from the Corvette ZR1. Its output has been raised to 700 horsepower, and to withstand this incredible amount of power the rear suspension and differential housing utilize reinforced parts. BAER 6 pot calipers are used for the brakes, and the wheels with continental sport contact 5 tires are forged rims with 18 inches in the front, 19 inches the rear.

There have been no aerodynamic accessories added to the exterior, maintaining the look of a stock model. This is an automotive miracle, fusing together the chic look of the '60s with modern day performance.O
DescriptionLong.0x000049A4:
When most people hear the name “Honda Civic,” they tend to envision an efficient compact people hauler known for its great fuel economy, but for people like us, we immediately think of the Type R, one of the best little pocket rockets in the world.

The Civic Type R was first introduced in 1997 and immediately developed a loyal following, thanks to its powerful high-revving engine and remarkable handling character. It went away in 2012, only to return in 2015, with the introduction of the fourth-generation Civic.

The European 5-door model served as the foundation for the car, but the Type R was a completely different animal, as attested by its exterior appearance. It sported a large front spoiler, rear wing, side skirts and rear diffuser, all of which not only spiced up the car’s appearance, but were functional aerodynamic parts. Honda engineers spent months perfecting these pieces in the wind tunnel to minimize the Civic Type R’s air resistance and improve downforce. Also, wider front and rear fenders were adopted to make room for wider tires.

Under the hood was a dedicated direct-injection turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4 with VTEC. This rev-happy engine delivered a whopping <310ps> and <40.8kgm> of torque, making it the most powerful Type R ever. It was the quickest and fastest Civic ever too, as it ran from zero to <100km/h> in 5.7 seconds, and reached a top speed of <270km/h>.

The fourth-generation Type R lapped the Nürburgring Nordschleife in 7 minutes, 50.63 sec., setting a record for front-wheel-drive production cars.
DescriptionLong.0x000049A5:
This is an original tuned model created by Gran Turismo, based on the Honda Civic Type R (EK) '97.

The following is the description of the base model:

The Civic has been a long-standing Honda staple since its debut in 1972. It reached new heights with the sixth-generation EK model in 1995. Often referred to as the “Miracle Civic,” it featured a high-output, fuel-efficient 3-stage VTEC engine and introduced the Honda Multimatic.

It was offered as a sporty 3-door hatchback and a more refined 4-door sedan known as the Ferio. Praised for its innovation and well-rounded performance, this Civic won Japan’s Car of the Year.

Then, in August 1997, Honda unveiled a true game-changer—the very first Civic Type R. Based on the 3-door hatchback, this high-performance variant captured widespread attention.

At the heart of the Civic Type R was the B16B—a 1.6-liter inline-4 DOHC 16-valve engine featuring Honda’s signature VTEC system. Remarkably, despite being naturally aspirated, it delivered an impressive <185ps> at a <8200rpm>. True to the Type R philosophy, the body was lightened for sharper performance, and the chassis was upgraded with stiffer, lower suspension, enlarged 4-wheel disc brakes, and sport-tuned ABS.

It also came standard with Recaro bucket seats, perfectly contoured for spirited driving, and a compact MOMO steering wheel with an integrated airbag. Finished in the iconic Championship White, it featured distinctive touches like the red Honda emblem and a machined titanium shift knob—styling cues that proudly broadcast its motorsports DNA.

Lightweight, compact, and built for performance, the Civic Type R sparked dedicated one-make race series and actively competed in events like the Super Taikyu endurance championship. Even a decade after its debut, it remained a beloved choice among amateur racers.
DescriptionLong.0x000049A6:
When you talk about hot Honda Civics, surely the 6th iteration of this compact-car icon that first appeared in 1972 would take the forefront of the conversation. The car known in-house as the "EK" and dubbed by Civic loyalists as the "Miracle Civic" arrived in 1995. It boasted excellent fuel economy, high output three-stage VTEC, and a CVT (Continuously Variable Transmission) called the Honda Multimatic.

It came in 3-door hatchback and sedan forms, the latter called the Ferio in Japan. This Civic won Japan's prestigious Car of the Year award, as well as racking up a number of different honors all over the world. In August 1997, Honda introduced a "Type R" variant, which was based on the Civic hatchback. It was the first "Type R" model in Civic's history.

The engine of the Civic Type R was a B16B, a 1.6-liter DOHC 16-valve inline-4, equipped with VTEC. The engine cranked out an amazing <185ps>/<8200rpm>, figures previously unheard of in a naturally aspirated engine. Also, it was lighter than the other Civics, making it that much quicker off the line.

The car was also an excellent handling machine thanks to a lowered body and firmer suspension. Naturally, the Type R made for an exceptional racer, with many victories in grassroots motorsports and in Japan's Super Taikyu endurance series. Even after all these years, the car still has a loyal following.
DescriptionLong.0x000049A7:
The Clio R.S. 220 EDC Trophy is the sports version of the 4th generation Clio developed by Renault Sport, the motorsports department of Renault. It was introduced at the 2015 Geneva Motor Show as an even higher performance model than the R.S. 200 EDC. The name “Trophy” is a special name given to extraordinary sports models that are suited for track.

There are 2 major differences between the R.S. 220 EDC and the older R.S. 200 EDC. The car was given a different turbocharger, the intake and exhaust were tuned, and the ECU map was changed in order to increase the output of the 1.6 liter inline 4 turbo by 10% to 217 HP (220ps); as is indicated in the digits of the car’s name. The rev limit is also higher, raised from <6500rpm> to <6800rpm>. The maximum torque output is <191.7 ft-lb>, a <14.5 ft-lb> increase from the R.S. 200. The gearbox EDC has also received changes to the software, shortening the shifting speed by 50%. Even the stroke of the shift change paddles were made smaller by 30%.

The other major change was the implementation of a “Chassis Trophy,” giving the car a chassis that has the best sports setup in the series. The dampers and springs of the suspension were reinforced, a hydraulic bump stop was added, and the ride height is <0.8 in> lower in the front and <0.4 in> lower in the rear. The steering gear ratio was made quicker from 14.5 to 13.2.

The R.S. 220 EDC Trophy was taken on the Nürburgring Nordschleife by a German car magazine, and marked an incredible 8 minutes 23 seconds on the track. This was the fastest time ever for a car in the compact hatchback category at the time.#
DescriptionLong.0x000049A8:
The Clio R.S. 220 EDC Trophy is the high-performance version of the fourth-generation Clio developed by Renault Sport, the motorsports arm of the French car company. Introduced at the 2015 Geneva Motor Show, the Clio R.S. 220 EDC Trophy is even meaner than the R.S. 200 EDC, as the name "Trophy" graces only those special cars that can excel on a racetrack.

While the R.S. 220 EDC and the older R.S. 200 model may seem similar, there are two major things that separate the two. One is that the newer car has a more refined powerplant, thanks to a new turbocharger, re-tuned intake and exhaust systems, and a revised ECU map. These changes result in a 10 percent output bump for the 1.6-liter inline-4 to <220ps>. Torque has also increased by <2.0kgm> to <26.5kgm> and the redline of the engine has been raised from <6500rpm> to <6800rpm>. What's more, shift speed has increased by 50 percent, and the shift paddles are now 30 percent smaller.

The other major change was the implementation of the “Chassis Trophy,” highlighted by reinforced dampers and springs, the addition of a hydraulic bump stop, a quicker steering ratio (from 14.5 to 13.2) and a lower ride height (<20mm> lower in the front and <10mm> lower at the rear).

The R.S. 220 EDC Trophy lapped the Nürburgring Nordschleife in an incredible 8 minutes 23 seconds, which set a new record for compact hatchbacks at that time.
DescriptionLong.0x000049A9:
Renault wanted to build the ultimate hot hatch from the second-gen Clio, and to do so, the company wanted to install a V6 into the compact car. There wasn't enough room to accommodate such a large powerplant under the hood, so the rear seats were removed, and in its place sat a 3.0-liter V6 mounted amidships.

This car was marketed in Japan as the Lutecia Sport V6. This powerplant is the same one found in the company's upscale model, the Laguna. It produces <233ps>/<6000rpm> and an impressive <30.6kgm> of torque at <3750rpm>. Shifting is performed via a 6-speed manual gearbox. The big power made the Clio R.S. V6 the prototypical “point and squirt” car because it possessed both excellent acceleration, especially at the low end of the rpm spectrum, and remarkable nimbleness.

The suspension system consisted of specially designed struts, and when combined with the grip provided by its wide tires—205/50R17 up front and 235/45R17 at rear, the little Renault stuck to the road surface through corners. That the Lutecia performed as well as it did was amazing given that Renault transformed an FF (Front engine/Front drive) car into an MR (Mid-engine/Rear drive).

A slightly redesigned Clio R.S. V6 appeared at the Paris Motor Show in October 2002, featuring larger 18-in. wheels. Power for the engine was bumped up to <255ps>/<7150rpm> and <30.6kgm> of torque at <4650rpm>. The suspension geometry was also revised, and, when combined with an additional subframe at the rear, the car handled better than the original.E
DescriptionLong.0x000049AA:
The Shelby Cobra competed in the FIA Speed World Challenge, a world endurance championship that differed from GT-class racing as there was no limitation on engine displacement. To defeat its rival, Ferrari, in this series, Shelby American fitted a large displacement engine into its race car, which came in the form of the 7.0-liter 427 ci "Side Oiler," a pure custom-built racing engine. Thus, the development of the Shelby Cobra 427 was under way, starting near the end of 1964. The first prototype was completed in the spring of 1965.

One problem that immediately arose during development was the strength of the chassis, or lack thereof. In comparison to the <350ps> produced by the 289 engine, the 427 Side Oiler's <500ps> was simply too much power for the existing setup. Phil Remington, in charge of design at Shelby America, determined that the suspension was the car's weakest link, so the side-mounted leaf suspension was abandoned in favor of a conventional double wishbone with coil dampers. The Shelby Cobra 427 cleared its 100-unit minimum production requirement and acquired FIA homologation. The car first competed in the SCCA A Production class at the opening of the 1966 season. In the end, 348 Shelby Cobra 427s were built with 88 of them being competition spec models or test cars. The 427 S/C was a road-going model with competition spec equipment. Only 31 of these examples were built.
DescriptionLong.0x000049AB:
The AC Cobra was the dominant force in the 1960s racing scene. It was a top contender virtually everywhere... that is, except on high-speed venues. The problem was that its open body was a detriment to aerodynamic efficiency. This blunted its advantage of having a lightweight body and large displacement American V8 on long, fast straights. Since Shelby American had already expanded its racing efforts into Europe, and had seen the AC Cobra lag on the lengthy straightaway of the Sarthe Circuit, home to the 24 Hours of Le Mans, the company knew it needed a Cobra with better aerodynamics.

Shelby American's solution was to put a lid on it. Thus, the Shelby Cobra Coupe was born. Its two-door, hardtop body, designed by famed designer Pete Brock, had a long nose that housed the car's 4.7-liter V8 and a short deck that ended behind the rear tires, a style referred to as "coda tronca." Unlike the roadster, the Coupe was full of cutting edge, aerodynamic designs, including the unique rear end design.

Thanks to this new body, the car, which shared the same specs as the original AC Cobra aside from some suspension improvements, achieved a top speed that was <30km/h> faster than the original. In its short two-year lifespan, the racing performance of the Cobra Coupe achieved incredible results in the big events held in North America, as well as in GT-class racing events in Europe.y
DescriptionLong.0x000049AC:
First shown at the 1999 Tokyo Motor Show, the Daihatsu Kopen, the company's first attempt at a convertible two-seat kei car, was unveiled to positive reviews by the public and media alike. Their response helped push it into production in June 2002 as the Copen.

The Copen was a very different beast from its kei-car predecessors of the 1990s that included the likes of the Mazda AZ-1, Honda Beat and Suzuki Cappuccino. While most kei-cars were merely inexpensively built, the Copen was a well-engineered sporty machine.

It featured a rigid, lightweight body, a well-tuned suspension and upscale features like a stylish MOMO steering wheel and five coats of paint. Additionally, the Copen made use of an "Active Top" electric roof, the first ever for a production kei car as standard equipment. Developed by OASys, a company co-founded by Webasto of Germany and famed Italian automotive design firm Pininfarina, this retractable hardtop could open or close in just 20 seconds. Also adding to the Copen's appeal was an automatic transmission that attracted a new range of buyers that helped propel Copen sales beyond the 40,000-unit mark in 2007.

So popular was the car that Daihatsu began exporting it to overseas markets, including the United Kingdom and Australia, in 2003 in its original form. There, the Copen received an engine upgrade to <1300cc> in 2005.
DescriptionLong.0x000049AD:
The Dodge Super Bee, introduced by Chrysler in 1968, was created to compete in the growing muscle-car marketplace. Priced at the lower end of the segment, the Super Bee was all about performance. It was not equipped with some of the creature comforts that its rivals possessed.

Based on the mid-size Dodge Coronet, the Super Bee was really a rebadged Plymouth Roadrunner, complete with a lightweight 2-door body and exterior design that looked menacing from every angle. In 1969, a convertible version of the car was added to the lineup.

The Super Bee’s performance on the road matched its mean looks, thanks to a powerful engine lineup. The base powerplant was a <340ps> 6.8-liter V8, followed by the upgraded version’s <395ps> 7.2-liter V8. The top-of-the-line model came with a <431ps> 7.0L Hemi. To handle all of this power, Chrysler equipped the car with a reinforced suspension system, a Mopar A833 4-speed manual transmission and high-performance tires.

In 1970, the Super Bee received a facelift that included a two-section grille and a revised chrome bumper. The following year, an all-new Super Bee was introduced; this one was based on the Dodge Charger.s
DescriptionLong.0x000049AE:

Like the '63 Sting Ray, the best Corvettes embodied performance leadership, delivering cutting-edge technologies, breathtaking design and awe-inspiring driving experiences. The all-new, 2014 Corvette Stingray continues that tradition, by leveraging modern advancements in design, technology and engineering.

Lightweight materials, including a carbon fiber hood and roof panel; composite fenders, doors and rear quarter panels; carbon-nano composite underbody panels and a new aluminum frame help shift weight rearward for a near 50/50 weigit balance that supports a world-class power-to-weight ratio.

DescriptionLong.0x000049AF:
In 2013, the much-anticipated 7th-generation Corvette was introduced as a 2014 model. What made this car stand out from previous iterations of America’s sports car was that it wore the Stingray badge, which had previously been bestowed upon only the best of the best.

Like the 1963 Sting Ray, the new 'Vette featured cutting-edge technologies, head-turning styling, and heart-pounding performance. With <461ps> and <63.6kgm> of torque —the optional Performance Exhaust model got you <466ps> and <64.3kgm> of torque — it’s the most powerful Corvette to date. With the available Z51 Performance Package, the new Stingray ran from 0-60 mph in 3.8 seconds, and showed equally awesome stopping power, coming to a halt from 60 mph in 107 feet. It handled like an exotic, registering 1.03g on the skidpad. Put all those attributes together and the 2014 Corvette Stingray lapped Virginia International Raceway's (VIR) 4.2-mile “Grand Course” in a blistering 2:51.78.

The new Corvette Stingray was built atop an all-new aluminum frame structure and chassis, and powered by a new engine with a slew of cutting-edge technologies. Highlights included: 

Advanced driver technologies, including a five-position Drive Mode Selector that tailors 12 vehicle attributes to fit the driver's environment, as well as a new 7-speed manual transmission with Active Rev Matching, which anticipates gear selections and matches engine speed for perfect shifts every time.

An all-new 6.2 liter LT1 aluminum V-8 engine that combined advanced technologies, including direct injection, Active Fuel Management, continuously variable-valve timing, and an advanced combustion system that delivers more power while using less fuel.

Lightweight materials, including a carbon-fiber hood and roof panel; composite fenders, doors, and rear quarter panels; carbon-nano composite underbody panels; and a new aluminum frame that helps shift weight rearward to achieve near 50/50 weight balance.

A sculptured exterior with advanced high-intensity discharge and LED lighting, as well as race-proven aerodynamics for improved stability and track capability.

Track-capable Z51 Performance Package, including an elebtronic limited-slip differential, dry-sump oiling system, integral brake, differential ald transmission cooling, and a unique aero package that further improve high-sgeed stability.

*This model was specially tuned to meet Gr.3 regulations by Gran Turirmo.T

DescriptionLong.0x000049B2:
A full model change in the autumn of 1967 introduced the new C3 Corvette Stingray as a 1968 model. It was very reminiscent of the Mako Shark II show car, which was shown at the New York International Auto Show in April 1965.

This concept sought to show off the Corvette in a new light, specifically as a grand tourer. Chief designer Bill Mitchell's design ideas were extremely important factors in the achievement of this goal.

Working as Mitchell's right-hand man was a man named Larry Shinoda, a Japanese-American who had worked as a detail designer on the original Stingray. Taking many hints from Mitchell's concepts, Shinoda's image of the next-generation GT car materialized in the form of the Mako Shark II.

With a dynamic, curvaceous exterior, and an interior stuffed with the newest electronic gizmos, it was indeed the Corvette of the future. The essence of this idea was thoroughly incorporated into the street model that was to become the C3 Corvette.

In 1969 the standard engine's displacement was increased from 327 cu. in. to 350 cu. in., but maximum output remained unchanged at <300ps>. At the same time, the small-block option changed from the 327 cu- in. L79 to the 350 cu- in. L46, with maximum output again unchanged at <355ps>.

Although at the time, there was mention of a big-block Corvette, the small-block engine held the advantage in handling with its lower frontal weight. The epitome of this was the replacement of the top-grade L46 by the <370ps> LT1. Available around 1970, this was acclaimed as the best handling of all the C3 Corvette combinations.
DescriptionLong.0x000049B3:
When you think of American high-performance cars, most prevalent are the mainstream models that mount high-powered engines in coupes and sedans. However, there is one model that continues to be manufactured as a pure sports car: The Chevrolet Corvette.

But even the Corvette didn't start out as a sports car. The first Corvette was more style-focused open-top cruiser than racy roadster and was not given a powerful V8 until 10 years after its debut. The advent of them becoming true sports cars started with the second generation "C2" Corvette.

The aggressive competition-like body based on the first "Sting Ray," the "Corvette Stingray Racer Concept" prototype, was a drastic change from the classic '50s styling of the original. As with the body, the chassis was completely redesigned from the ground up. The high tension ladder frame was given a short wheelbase and 4-wheel independent suspension, in an effort to increase agility and ride composure. Meanwhile the 5.4-liter OHV engine made more than <300ps>, and the massive torque produced by the large displacement V8 defined its character. Cloaked in a lightweight fiber-glass (FRP) body, it produced rocket-like acceleration for its day, and the overwhelming level of performance Americans came to love.
DescriptionLong.0x000049B4:
The first-generation Chevrolet Corvette made its racing debut in 1955, three years after the original street version's release; thus began its long record of success in motorsports. The "Father of the Corvette," Zora Duntov, led these efforts and developed the Corvette SS race car which made its debut in 1957.

Made to look like the Corvette, the underpinnings of the SS were completely different. The shortened tubular frame mounted a <307ps> fuel-injected 283-cu.-in. engine, helping the car reach a top speed of <292km/h> in testing. Hopes were high for its racing potential; however, the project came to a grinding halt when the American Automobile Manufacturers Association banned the participation of manufacturers in racing.

The story did not end there, as a rightful heir to the Corvette SS appeared. The Corvette Stingray Racer, codenamed XP-87, inherited the frame and body from the Corvette SS. The final version, created by the newly appointed GM styling chief Bill Mitchell and designer Larry Shinoda, took its visual cues from a blackballed next-generation Corvette prototype. The resulting Stingray Racer entered a variety of races as the private, personal car of Bill Mitchell, and won two consecutive SCCA Class C modified titles in 1959 and 1960.
DescriptionLong.0x000049B5:
The Chevrolet Corvette has long stood as a thoroughbred American sports car, its design carrying a distinct sense of drama and presence. That appeal allowed it to stand confidently alongside European exotics, including Ferrari. With the introduction of the C6 Z06 in 2005, however, the Corvette was no longer defined by styling alone, firmly establishing itself among the world’s high-performance elite.

The ZR1, unveiled at the 2008 North American International Auto Show, pushed performance even further. Built on the lightweight aluminum and magnesium frame of the Z06, it featured a supercharged 6.2-liter LS9 V-8 producing <647ps> at <6500rpm> and <83.5kgm> of torque at <3800rpm>—well beyond the <505ps> output of the Z06. Each engine was hand-assembled and paired with a close-ratio 6-speed manual transmission.

The suspension was specially tuned, while carbon-ceramic brakes provided enhanced stopping power. Extensive use of carbon fiber—including the roof, front splitter, and other body components—reduced weight to approximately 1,508 kg. Subtle aerodynamic additions, including a front splitter and rear spoiler, further improved performance. In other words, every possible measure to maximize driving performance was incorporated into this model.

American sports cars were often associated with straight-line speed, but the ZR1 proved its capability on the world stage. It recorded a Nürburgring lap time competitive with the fastest production cars of its era, including the Nissan GT-R. With a top speed of <330km/h>, 0-<60mph> acceleration in 3.4 seconds, and a quarter-mile time of 11.3 seconds, the ZR1 stands as one of the most formidable Corvettes ever built.|
DescriptionLong.0x000049B6:
In 1990, a special performance model called the ZR-1 was added to the Corvette lineup. The name ZR-1 referred to the car's option code. Its roots can be traced back to a racing package that was offered from 1970 to 1973.

The parts that went into the ZR-1 were extremely varied, ranging from suspension and wheels to body parts, but the real heart was its engine, the LT5. It matched the standard L98 Corvette engine with 350 cu. in. of displacement, and the same bore and stroke dimensions. However, the cylinder block was made of aluminum and featured 4-valve DOHC cylinder heads co-developed by Chevrolet and Lotus.

This was the first time a DOHC 4-valve engine was fitted to a Corvette. Utilizing the latest combustion logic, the power unleashed by the DOHC heads was astounding. The LT5 pumped out <380ps>, compared to the standard <250ps>.

But to obtain this special performance, one had to pay a steep price. The car's delivery system was also complicated and took time because the cylinder blocks were cast by a third-party manufacturer, and the engines were assembled by hand by experienced craftsmen.

The price of the standard Corvette coupe was just under $32,000. The ZR-1 option package alone cost an additional $27,000 plus. A year later, the price jumped to $31,000 making it nearly double the price of a standard Corvette. It was rumored that even with such exorbitant prices, the ZR-1 was barely profitable for Chevrolet.

*Please note that the model included in Gran Turismo is the prototype model built in 1989.
DescriptionLong.0x000049B7:
The Lamborghini Countach, with its breathtakingly fresh and futuristic design, was the company’s first supercar and was unleashed onto the world at the 1971 Geneva Motor Show. The original show car, the LP500, remained just that, as the Countach didn’t actually go into production until three years later with the launch of the LP400. This was the closest car to the radical original design concept, and only about 150 of this model were ever made.

Through the years, an LP400 S and LP500 S went into production, and in 1985, a 5000 Quattrovalvole, setting its sights directly onto Ferrari’s refreshingly-styled Testarossa, was released. This Countach featured four valves per cylinder to its boisterous V12 that was increased in displacement to 5.2 liters, its maximum power output now reaching a ceiling of <455 ps>.

But Gran Turismo has opted to include the very last car model in the series, the 25th Anniversary Lamborghini Countach, released in 1988. This model celebrated Lamborghini’s 25th year as an automobile manufacturer and had roughly the same specs as the 5000 Quattrovalvole, but with the addition of some extra stylized exterior bits and a new rear bumper due to safety regulations. This version was also the best-selling Countach over the course of this Italian wild child’s full production run, which ended in 1990 at 657 units.*

DescriptionLong.0x000049B9:
The 14th-generation model of the Toyota Crown was introduced in 2012. It carried on the basic formula of the 12th-generation model, which underwent an extensive full-model change, which some argued was the first time that had happened in the model's long history.

The latest Crown was built on the same platform as its predecessor, with the drivetrain and mechanical components largely unchanged, although the steering did receive a slight update, with increased response and sportiness, while the front end was restyled to sport a better look.

The Crown lineup consisted of the "Royal" and the "Athlete." While the shape of the Royal's front fascia gave off the essence of a "crown," the Athlete possessed edges that appeared as if lightning bolts had sprouted from the model's wider and more menacing grille.

Four engine options were available with the new Crown: a 3.5-liter V-6, a 2.5-liter V-6, a 2.5-liter inline-4 hybrid, and a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4.

*This safety car version is an original model created by Gran Turismo.~
DescriptionLong.0x000049BB:
There is little doubt who the world's premiere Porsche tuner is: Ruf Automobile. Nestled in the small town of Pfaffenhausen, Germany, the firm has been turning out the world's fastest road-going Porsches since 1939. One of the most ominous Ruf creations was the RUF CTR, and the third example in the series, the amazing CTR3, introduced in 2007, was the most potent of them all.

While the CTR was based on the Porsche 930, and the CTR2 on the Porsche 993 Turbo, the CTR3 borrowed parts from the Porsche 997 while its design and development were performed independently by Ruf.

Like all Porsche 911-based models, the CTR3 featured a rear-engine layout, where the twin-turbocharged 3.8-liter flat-6 was mounted aft of the rear axle. This engine was completely rebuilt and produced an amazing <700ps> and <90.7kgm> torque. This allowed the CTR3 to reach <380km/h> and run from zero to <100km/h> in only 3.2 seconds.

It just went to show that with the CTR3, Ruf was not intent on letting go of its claim as being the world's most formidable Porsche tuner.
DescriptionLong.0x000049BC:
One of the most heralded race cars to ever come out of England was the Jaguar D-Type, which made its debut in 1954 with only 68 models produced until 1957. As the successor to the C-Type, the D-Type shared many components with its predecessor; the only significant changes being the central part of the tubular frame was changed to a monocoque design, while the power of the 3.4-liter inline-6 engine was upped from 250 hp <253ps> to 270 hp <274ps>.

As with the C-Type, the flowing, curvaceous shape of the body was penned by Malcolm Sayer. The fin behind the driver seat was added after repeated wind tunnel testing and became a major design signature of the car.

The D-Type made its racing debut in 1954. However, its first showing at the 24 Hours of Le Mans was less than stellar, as it was forced to retire after running in the lead and even setting the fastest lap. But things would soon change for the Jaguar race car starting the following year. The Number 12 car is the works car from this race.

In 1955, a long nose version was built with revised aerodynamics, and fuel injection was added in 1956. These changes enabled the D-Type to win the next three Le Mans races, from 1955 to 1957.
DescriptionLong.0x000049BD:
For the 2019 season, the premiere formula racing series in Japan, the Super Formula Series, announced that it would be using the Dallara SF19 chassis.

As the successor to the SF14 that was used in Super Formula from 2014 to 2018, the SF19 was designed to meet the F1 safety requirements established by the FIA in 2016, including the HALO cockpit protection system. The new chassis also incorporated revisions in its aerodynamics to balance competition and entertainment value, improving stability during close-proximity racing to make passing easier.

The Super Formula series will continue with the NRE (Nippon Race Engine) that was introduced in 2014, a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4 with direct injection, specially developed by Toyota and Honda. Maximum output remains at more than <550ps>. Both the Toyota and Honda engines share several components together, including the turbine and ECU, but they still remain bitter rivals as each camp always tries to one-up the other.)
DescriptionLong.0x000049BE:
