The car was tuned by Abarth, which had just been acquired by the FIAT Group. The prototype featured a heavily modified version of the base <903cc> OHV inline-4 engine, with displacement increased to <982cc>, resulting in <108ps>. This allowed the car to reach a top speed of <208km/h>.

The production model retained the <982cc> engine, but it was detuned to <58ps> to enhance everyday usability. Despite the decrease, it still produced 20 percent more power than the base engine.

Abarth continued to make numerous improvements to the A112's performance. In 1975, engine displacement was increased to <1050cc>, boosting output to <71ps>. In 1979, the transmission was upgraded from a 4-speed to a 5-speed unit, 

Although production ceased in 1985, the car remains a favorite among enthusiasts for its uniquely spirited and energetic character.
DescriptionLong.0x00005141:
Introduced in 1963, the FIAT Abarth 595 was a high-performance version of the second-generation FIAT 500 tuned by Abarth.

While the base FIAT 500 featured a <496cc> air-cooled 2-cylinder engine, the Abarth version received comprehensive upgrades. Displacement was increased to <594cc>, complemented by enhanced intake and exhaust flow. These upgrades delivered a significant performance boost, with peak output rising from <18ps> to <27ps> and top speed increased from <95km/h> to <120km/h>. The transformation made the Abarth variant a favorite among young enthusiasts who craved more power.

Then, in 1964, Abarth introduced an even more finely tuned version of the 595. This car was called the 595 Esseesse.

The 595 Esseesse utilized the same basic engine as its predecessor, but compression ratio was increased and a larger diameter carburetor was installed, resulting in <32ps> and a top speed of <130km/h>.

Thanks to the newfound power, the 595 series enjoyed great success in the under-<600cc>-class of racing all over Europe.
DescriptionLong.0x00005142:
The BMW 3.0 CS, a luxury sports coupe developed from the 2800 CS, which was released in 1968, picked up where the 2800 CS left off. 

Powering the original 2800CS was a 2.8-liter inline-6 that was called "the Big Six." For the 3.0 CS, engine displacement was increased to 3.0 liters, increasing power to <180ps>/<26.0kgm>. To improve stopping power, BMW equipped the 3.0 CS with 4-wheel disc brakes. 

The car's performance was so exceptional that BMW decided to take the Big Six racing, so it built a homologation model with significantly reduced weight. This version, called the 3.0 CSL (the "L" stood for "leicht," which in English means "light"), weighed 200 kg less than the base CS, making it an absolute road rocket.
DescriptionLong.0x00005143:
The top-of-the-line version of Subaru's popular BRZ sports car was the BRZ STI Sport, introduced in 2017. The STI in its name referred to the company's motorsports division, Subaru Tecnica International, which gave the BRZ plenty of special touches that distinguished it from the base model.

The exterior featured a unique front bumper and fender garnishes, providing more muscle to the compact rear-drive machine. In the cabin, more luxury and exclusivity was added, including a Bordeaux red color scheme, available only on STI Sports models, and leather and alcantara seats.

STI made no major engine tweaks, but it did add flexible V bars and draw stiffeners to enhance rigidity. Also, the suspension system was tuned with Sachs shocks and springs, which helped provide the car with razor sharp steering responses and excellent handling.
DescriptionLong.0x00005144:
When the Carrera GT was introduced in 2003, it became an instant collector's car, not only because it was one of the most exotic cars Porsche had ever produced, but only a total of 1270 units were manufactured.

Unlike the 911, Porsche's signature model, the Carrera GT had a mid-engine layout. Tucked behind the cabin was a 5.7-liter V-10 that was originally designed for LMP endurance racing. The naturally aspirated engine produced <612ps> and <60.2kgm> of torque that came mated to a 6-speed manual transmission. With a curb weight of only <1380kg> — carbon fiber was not used sparingly in the Carrera GT — the car was a virtual road rocket, going from zero to <100km/h> in a scant 3.9 seconds and reaching a top speed of more than <330km/h>. 

In 2006, the Carrera GT was discontinued, but it remains one of the most alluring Porsches of not only its generation, but of all time.
DescriptionLong.0x00005145:
The Mercedes-Benz CLK-GTR was created to compete in the ITC (International Touring Car Championship) after it replaced the FIA GT Championships in 1997. Developed in just 128 days by the company's motorsports and tuning division, AMG, the CLK-GTR got off to a somewhat rocky start in its race career, but rebounded quickly, winning six out of its first 11 races, claiming both the drivers' title and the constructor's championship in its first season.

The following year saw a new, evolved version of the car called the CLK-LM. The most noticeable change was the engine. Replacing the V-12 was a new V-8 that made the car lighter and enhanced its longitudinal balance. The radiator was moved from the front of the car to the sides so a lower hood could be implemented, thus improving the car's aerodynamics, while a new pushrod-type suspension gave it superior handling performance.

The CLK-LM made its debut at the 1998 Le Mans 24-hour race. While it failed to win that race, it did dominate every race of the FIA GT series, claiming the series championships with Klaus Ludwig and Ricardo Zonta at the wheel.
DescriptionLong.0x00005146:
One of the most recognizable classic cars today is the Aston Martin DB5, and that's because it has been the automobile of choice of a certain fictitious super spy named James Bond. First appearing in the Bond film Goldfinger, the DB5, introduced in 1963, was built by Italian coachbuilder Carrozzeria Touring using Touring's patented "Superleggera" super light construction methods.

The DB5 was powered by a tuned version of the DB4's inline-6, but with displacement increased to 4.0 liters, it produced a hearty <285.9ps>, while the high-performance Vantage model pumped out <318.4ps>. These numbers exceeded the output of some V-12-equipped sports cars of the day, making Aston Martin owner Sir David Brown ("DB") one of the most significant automobile manufacturers of his time.
DescriptionLong.0x00005147:
A driving force for Pontiac in the mid-1960s and once vice president of General Motors, John Z. DeLorean made the bold choice of starting his own car company at the end of the 1970s.

DeLorean Motor Company (DMC) was established in Ireland in 1975. Its first serious production model was the DMC-12.

DeLorean's objective was to produce a reasonable, stylish sports car; however, as his new company did not have the expertise to develop such a car, the design of the DMC-12 had to be outsourced.

DeLorean turned to Lotus to develop the chassis, while Italdesign was tasked to pen the exterior and interior styling. The DMC-12 rode on a backbone chassis and came powered by a PRV SOHC V-6 that produced <130ps>, but what drew the most attention about the car were its shiny stainless steel body and gull-wing doors.

DeLorean sold 6500 units of the DMC-12 in its first year, but a public scandal and other bad headlines forced the company into bankruptcy in 1983. By this time, 8500 units of the car had been sold. 

After the entire inventory of DMC-12s were shipped from Ireland to the U.S., they were managed by a newly established DeLorean Motor Car Company that specialized in tuning the engine to <200ps>. These DeLorean cars are referred to as the DMC-12 Series 2.|
DescriptionLong.0x00005148:
Ferrari unveiled its mighty new flagship, the F12berlinetta, in 2012 at the Geneva Motor Show. The successor to the 599 GTB Fiorano featured a newly-designed base structure whose space frame and body shell combined 12 different types of aluminum alloys. The front mid-mounted engine came in the form of a naturally aspirated <6262cc> V-12 producing <740ps> and <70.5kgm> of peak torque, making it the most powerful Ferrari road car to date.

Impressive numbers, to be sure, but Ferrari spent a majority of its development effort on the car’s architecture. The F12berlinetta was <47mm> shorter, <20mm> narrower and <63mm> lower than its predecessor, with a wheelbase that measured <30mm> less. The engine sat <30mm> lower than the 599, and the dual clutch 7-speed F1-matic gearbox utilized a transaxle layout—both of these features helped to lower the center of gravity by <25mm> and established a nearly ideal front/rear weight ratio of 46:54.

On the road, the F12berlinetta, despite its elegant good looks, was an absolute beast. It ran from zero to <100km/h> in a phenomenal 3.1 seconds, getting to <200km/h> in just 8.5, and topping out at a blurring <340km/h>. With its improved handling balance, it set a new fastest road car lap around the Fiorano test track, besting the 599 GTO by a full second.

With refined aerodynamics, advanced electronic devices and a brake cooling system that trickled down from its Formula 1 race car, this prancing horse deserved to be the flagship for what is arguably the most revered and recognized company in automotive history.
DescriptionLong.0x00005149:
In 1969, Nissan completely transformed the Fairlady brand from that of a classic open-top roadster into a classy fixed-roof sports car that went by the name 240Z in many parts of the world. A performance-oriented version of this car was created, called the Z 432. 

The car's name referred to its engine, namely its 4 valves, 3 carburettors and 2 camshafts. While the base car came with the L20, a SOHC inline-6, the Z 432 was powered by the L20, which was in fact a detuned version of the <220ps> GR8 engine used in the R380 prototype race car. In the Z 432, it produced <160ps>, which was the same as the previously released Skyline GT-R version.

This made the special Z car quick — a 0-<400m> time of 15.8s and top speed of <210km/h> — making for an ideal race car, but only a limited number of a pure race versions of the car, called the Z 432R, were made. It featured fibrerlass and acrylic components that decreased its weight by <100kg>. Today, the car is a prized collector's item with an example rumored to have fetched $800,000 at auction. .
DescriptionLong.0x0000514A:
While the Focus is mostly known as a friendly everyday commuter, Ford has traditionally mixed in a high-performance version called the RS that catered directly to enthusiasts.

The fourth-generation model, which made its debut in 2018, was no different, but this time, the Focus RS was offered with AWD. With the new RS, drivers could adjust the torque distribution between the front and rear wheels, from 0:100 to 100:0, meaning it could be driven in pure front-drive or rear-drive form. Thanks to the rear axle's twin-clutch system that functions as an LSD, the driver could choose from several driving modes, including "Track" and "Drift." 

Under the hood was the company's EcoBoost 2.3-liter inline-4 tuned to produce an impressive <350ps> and <44.8kgm>, thanks to new turbocharger and larger intercooler. This allowed the car to run to <100km/h> in 4.7s and reach a top speed of <266km/h>, making this Ford one of the hottest American hatches of all time.
DescriptionLong.0x0000514B:
The second-generation Ford GT, introduced in 2015, came equipped with compact twin-turbo V-6 that allowed the car to spring to 60 mph in about 3.0 seconds and reach a top speed of <348km/h>, making it a legitimate super car and a worthy successor to the classic GT40 of yesteryear.

Like the GT40, the GT shined on the race track. Under the Chip Ganassi Racing and Ford factory team banner, it scored several victories in the World Endurance Championship (WEC) that included the 2016 24 Hours of Le Mans, as well as winning in IMSA, taking three race wins in 2016, two in 2017, five in 2018 and three in 2019. In 2018, after winning the 24 Hours of Daytona, the GT's strong performance that season handed Ford the manufacturers title in the GT-LM class.
DescriptionLong.0x0000514C:
Only 32 examples of the Ferrari FXX K were produced, meaning that it became an instant collector's item when it was introduced in 2014. Developed for track use only by Corso Clienti, the FXX K was based on the LaFerrari super car with various improvements to .

The "K" on its name stood for "HY-KERS," Ferrari's Hybrid Kinetic Energy Recovery system, similar to the KERS systems used on Ferrari's Formula 1 cars. Under the FXX K's hood was LeFerrari's 6.3-liter V-12 tuned to produce <860ps> combined with a <190ps> HY-KERS electric motor, totaling an output of <1050ps>.

In 2017, Ferrari introduced the FXX K Evo, whose aerodynamics enhancements resulted in 23 percent more downforce than the standard FXX K and 75 percent more than the La Ferrari. It generated up to <640kg> of additional weight at 200 km/h, making it one of the most potent supercars ever created by the company.K
DescriptionLong.0x0000514D:
From the very beginning, the base model of the Subaru Impreza was a 4-door sedan; however, when the third-generation model was introduced in 2007, Subaru threw the world a curve by offering the 5-door hatchback as the base model. Thus, the high-performance version of the car, the Impreza WRX STI that appeared in October of the same year, wore a 5-door body.

Still, many preferred the 3-box styling of the sedan because of its clean shape and long history as the brand's defining model. To satisfy these customers, Subaru introduced the much-anticipated WRX STI 4-door sedan to the public in July 2010. Under the hood resided the same Japan-market powerplant as the 5-door, a twin-scroll turbocharged 2.0-liter flat-4 that produced <308ps> and <43.0kgm> of torque. The new sedan stretched longer than its 5-door counterpart by <165mm>, most of this due to a longer rear end where a large wing was installed. Because of the different body style, the 4-door had a structural and aerodynamic advantage over the 5-door, making it faster on long straights.

The car's engine and chassis have been tuned in accordance with the high level of quality befitting a car wearing the STI badge. It exhibited little turbo lag, while the suspension displayed rock-solid stability through turns and an even ride quality. The car's prowess was unleashed in April 2010 on the North Loop of the Nürburgring, the main testing ground for Subaru in Europe, where former WRC champion Tommi Makinen, who once drove the WRC Impreza race car, lapped the 12.9-mile course in an amazing 7 minutes 55 seconds.
DescriptionLong.0x0000514E:
One year after the potent Spec C was introduced, Subaru wasted no time finessing the look of the new Impreza by taking a scalpel to the car's front end after only two years on the market. The round headlights were a bust as it alienated many loyal buyers, so the company replaced them with more conventional-looking tear-drop shaped ones.

The car's overall aerodynamics were also improved, thanks to developmental work performed by SWRT (Subaru World Rally Team). The team also improved the response of the boxer powerplant, raising peak torque to <40.2kgm>. The new exhaust system, which was originally developed for the 2003 Legacy, was more efficient, too. Of particular note was a new center differential that featured an automatic mode. This system managed the distribution of torque between the front and rear wheels through the center differential, allowing for maximum traction through all variety of corners.

The car's new handling prowess demanded more grip, so wider tires were used in 2004. This year also saw the torque figure of the flat-4 climb yet again, to <42.0kgm>. By this time, the Impreza WRX had caught the attention of performance enthusiasts everywhere, and in 2003, the car finally made its way to U.S. shores. Soon thereafter, Mitsubishi brought the Lancer Evolution to the U.S., and the two Japanese rally icons waged war on a new battleground, America.3
DescriptionLong.0x0000514F:
The Jaguar Vision Gran Turismo SV, an all-electric virtual race car created by Jaguar Special Vehicle Operations, was a radical interpretation of what an electric Jaguar of tomorrow could be.

Developed from the dramatic Jaguar Vision Gran Turismo Coupé of 2019, and fusing the spirit of the iconic C- and D-Type, the Vision Gran Turismo SV artfully blends the new with old. The car's sweeping body and perfectly balanced proportions offer the ultimate in aerodynamics. Highlights include the prominent front splitter, a purposefully-sculpted underbody, rear Venturi and a large rear wing with deployable elements.

The state-of-the-art lithium-ion battery pack, packaged around the cabin to enable ideal front/rear weight distribution, is cooled by a liquid nitrogen system that ensures every cell delivers maximum performance even under the most extreme race conditions.

The engineers successfully integrated elements of Jaguar’s I-TYPE 5 Formula E race car to the Vision Gran Turismo SV. Four powerful, compact electric motors help the car reach a top speed of more than 255 mph (approximately <410km/h>). The car also gives off a mean, distinctive sound to convey its powerful nature, one that reflects its true racing DNA.

Authentically yet futuristically Jaguar, the Vision Gran Turismo SV was designed and engineered to take the performance of the already potent Jaguar Vision Gran Turismo Coupé to the next level.h
DescriptionLong.0x00005150:
Automobili Lamborghini made a bold entrance into the world of virtual racing with a machine crafted to stir the soul of every Vision Gran Turismo enthusiast. Born from passion and brought to life by the expert hands of the Centro Stile team in Sant’Agata Bolognese, under the guidance of Head of Design Mitja Borkert, the Lampborghini Lambo V12 Vision Gran Turismo is a pure expression of Lamborghini’s design DNA.

What began as a series of sketches evolved into a 1:3 scale digital model, ultimately earning the approval of both Kazunori Yamauchi and Borkert.  The full-scale version was completed between 2018 and 2019 by a team driven by creativity and technical precision.

A single look at the Lamorghini Lambo V12 Vision Gran Turismo reveals its purpose.  Sculpted like a futuristic work of art, it embodies sharp, aerodynamic flair, while remaining rooted in engineering excellence.

From the outset, this was envisioned as a virtual race machine, and that intent shaped everything from its radical single-seat layout to its pilot-focused cabin.  Stripped down and purpose-built, the cabin is designed entirely around the player’s experience. The central driving position, reminiscent of Formula and endurance racers, emphasizes immersion. A digital cockpit, complete with augmented reality and voice control, reinforces the sensation of being in command.

Power comes from the same heart as the Lamborghini Sián FKP 37—a mid-mounted V-12 paired with a supercapacitor hybrid system. Producing more than <830.4ps>, it delivers amazing performance, and a rich sound that elevates the virtual driving experience. The engine is always on display, exposed and ever-inspiring.

The design stays true to Lamborghini’s unmistakable design language, centered around its signature one-line silhouette. Its overall architecture echoes the bold DNA first defined by the iconic Lamborghini Countach in 1971. Influences from Marcello Gandini’s visionary work are evident throughout. Particularly in the side profile, it draws inspiration from the radical 1970 Bertone Stratos Zero concept. From every angle, the car displays Lamborghini’s hallmark graphical elements: upsilon motifs, hexagonal forms, and “Y”-shaped front lights that foreshadow the brand’s future lighting identity."
DescriptionLong.0x00005151:
The Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution IX MR GSR was the updated version of the Lancer Evolution IX GSR that appeared a year prior. Although the two cars look nearly identical, numerous refinements were made to the 2006 model. Although the car's engine specs remained largely unchanged, the MIVEC variable valve timing system was retuned, the standard specification turbine wheel was changed to a titanium-aluminum alloy, and the compressor inlet diameter was downsized. Along with other minor improvements, this resulted in sharper engine response and faster acceleration. 

The suspension system was also enhanced, with high spring rate Eibach coils combined with Bilstein dampers. The electronically controlled Super AYC 4WD system was reprogrammed to focus on cornering ability. There were also refinements to the aerodynamics with the shape of the front bumper being changed to reduce lift.

The" MR" of its name stood for Mitsubishi Racing. Throughout the company's history, this designation was given to its highest performing models. For the Lancer Evolution, the MR name first appeared in the VIII lineup, making this IX the second MR model in the car's history.

This model represented the culmination of development on the third-generation Lancer Evolution, and it was the last to be equipped with the legendary 4G63 engine.
DescriptionLong.0x00005152:
The Mercedes AMG GT R made its debut in 2016 as a high performance version of the AMG GT introduced in 2014. While it was officially designated as a road car, it was in fact a race car in street-car clothing. 

The first thing to catch the eye on the AMG GT R were the vertical accents on the grille, reminiscent of those of the 300SL that won the 1952 Carrera Panamericana Mexico. Other notable features of the exterior included the adjustable rear wing and the flared fenders. 

Under the sheet metal, many of the car's components were swapped for carbon-fiber pieces, including the roof, front fenders and torque tube. This car was also the first Mercedes AMG model with 4-wheel steering. Under the hood, the car's twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter
V-8 was retuned to produce <585ps> and <71.3kgm>, allowing the AMG GT R to run from 0-<100km/h> in a lightning quick 3.6 seconds and reach a top speed of <318km/h>. 
`
DescriptionLong.0x00005153:
The BAC Mono, a sports car produced by British manufacturer Briggs Automotive Company since 2009, was the realization of the Briggs brothers' vision of "a road vehicle that offers the most authentic and pure driving experience possible while implementing the very latest in racing technology."

The car's most notable element was its formula car-style single seat design. However, unlike modern formula cars that are typically built on a carbon monocoque, the BAC Mono employed a more classical tubular frame design with a carbon-fiber body shell. Both the front and rear suspensions consisted of a double wishbone pushrod design.

The engine, situated behind the driver, came in the form of a Cosworth-tuned Ford Duratec 2.5-liter inline-4 that produced <309ps> and <31.4kgm>. It came mated to a race-specification 6-speed sequential transmission.

The BAC Mono was a remarkably lightweight car, tipping the scales at a very lean <580kg>, making its performance on par with F3 Formula racers of its day. Its performance numbers were awe-inspiring: a zero-to-60-mph time of 2.8 seconds and a top speed of <274km/h>.t
DescriptionLong.0x00005154:
The Polo, one of the core models in Volkswagen's lineup, has been considered a benchmark for B-segment cars around the world, and the fifth-generation model, introduced at the 2009 Geneva Motor Show was no exception.

The new Polo featured bold styling cues that differentiated it from other B-segment entries. It was also greener than its predecessor, thanks to a smaller engine and a super efficient 7-speed DSG transmission. The sporty GTI model made its debut in 2010, equipped with a new 1.4-liter direct injection inline-4 that came with both a turbo and supercharger. It produced <179ps>/<25.5kgm> that allowed the GTI to run from zero to <100km/h> in 6.9 seconds and reach a top speed of <225km/h>. What's more, fuel economy was rated at <16.6 km/L>, the best ever for a Polo.

With ground holding improvements including sports suspension and electronic devices that perform the same function as a limited-slip differential, the Polo GTI was one of the best handling machines in its segment, with some even claiming that it was right up there with its bigger brother, the vaunted Golf GTI.

In 2014, the GTI model received a facelift. One of the most notable changes is the new engine. Now featuring a <400cc> larger 1.8L inline-4 turbo engine, the maximum power output had increased to <192ps>. Extra power isn't the only difference, as the fuel efficiency had also been greatly improved, consuming much less fuel than the 1.4L GTI.
DescriptionLong.0x00005155:
As the name implies, the Audi R8 LMS Evo is an evolved version of the R8 LMS, a GT3-regulation race car based on the production R8 code named the Type 42. Introduced in 2009, it shined on the race track for six years, until an all-new R8 production car, the Type 45, made its debut.

What separated the R8 LMS from its production-car sibling was its superior cooling and improved aerodynamics. The front grille and rear bumper were enlarged, while air channels were added next to the headlights to provide extra cooling for the engine. The front canard wings were enlarged to provide extra downforce.

The 5.2-liter V-10 of the previous car was carried over, producing <585ps> and <56kgm>, but with curb weight reduced by <25kg> to <1200kg>, the new R8 LMS Evo was quicker and more agile than its predecessor.

Introduced at the 2018 Paris Motor Show, the R8 LMS Evo competed in and won the Gulf 12-hour race at the end of that same year.
DescriptionLong.0x00005156:
For years, Gran Turismo handed out its "Best in Show" award at the SEMA show, a giant aftermarket convention that takes place annually in Las Vegas, Nevada. In 2014, the 12th Best in Show award went to the 1970 Chevrolet Camaro SS "Rampage," built by muscle-car chassis specialists Roadster Shop of Illinois, United States.

True to its name, the car looked mean from every angle. Bulging fender flares at both the front and rear gave it a wide, menacing stance, while a large front spoiler and rear wing hinted of the prowess underneath the hood, which was a 7.0-liter LS7 tuned to produce <750ps> and mounted <13cm> rearward to improve weight distribution. 

Perhaps the most notable aspect of the car was its rebuilt chassis, which came with a roll cage and plenty of carbon-fiber and aluminum components. Also, the suspension was converted to an inboard cantilever design, which thoroughly impressed the Gran Turismo team and earned the car its distinct recognition.
DescriptionLong.0x00005157:
Introduced in 2011, the Mazda RX-8 Spirit R was the final special edition model of the RX-8 that was first released in 2003.

The RX-8 had two distinct personalities, depending on the gearbox you chose. Cars equipped with the 6-speed manual drove like a pure sport car, with brisk acceleration and more driver control, while those with the 6-speed automatic essentially behaved like luxury grand tourers. The Spirit R equipped with the 6-speed manual was based on the sporty Type RS, and featured extra aero parts and a sporty suspension setup, complete with Bilstein dampers. The automatic Spirit R was based on the Type E and included luxury accoutrements, such as leather seats. The car's Renesis rotary engine produced 235HP and 159 ft.-lb. of torque. 

The lifespan of the Spirit R was short-lived, as Mazda discontinued the RX-8 in June 2012. Because of that, initial orders for the Spirit R exceeded the intended batch of 1000 units, so Mazda produced another 1000 to meet demand.[
DescriptionLong.0x00005158:
In May 1988, the fifth-generation S13 Silvia stole market share away from the Honda Prelude and gained immediate popularity. This is because of its front-engine/rear-drive layout and fun-to-drive nature, but the main reason was the car's elegant styling. 

Under the hood was the CA18, a 1.8-liter inline-4, but it was later replaced by the SR20, a 2.0-liter DOHC inline-4. The premium K's model came turbocharged, producing <205ps> and <28.0kgm> of torque, while the Q's and J's remained naturally aspirated, rated at <140ps> and <18.2kgm>. The front suspension consisted of MacPherson struts up front and a multi-link setup at rear. Nissan's 4-wheel steering system, Super HICAS, was available as an option.

Thanks in part to the car's light weight — it tipped the scales at a lean <1170kg> — the turbocharged K's was quick off the line and made for an ideal drift machine. It was also a huge favorite among tuners, especially because the CA18DET could easily deliver <300ps> after a few tweaks. In fact, the S15 proved more popular to drifters and tuners than Nissan's signature FR sports car, the Z.
DescriptionLong.0x00005159:
The roots of the Shelby GT350R date back to 1965, when Ford commissioned Carol Shelby to build a car to compete in the SCCA (Sports Car Club of America). Based on the first-generation Mustang, the GT350R was sold as a road car because the SCCA allowed only minor modifications for its competition cars. Still, the car dominated its class, gaining instant recognition.

Fast forward to 2016, when the Shelby 350R based on the seventh-generation Mustang, made its debut as road car that was race ready, like the original model. Its naturally-aspirated 5.2-liter V-8 was tuned to produce <533ps> and <59.3kgm> and was mated to a 6-speed manual transmission.

The reinforced chassis featured Ford's MagneRide suspension system, which detected road conditions and adjusted damping strength using magnetorheological fluid. Also, to reduce weight, the 2+2 layout of the stock Mustang was converted into that of a two-seater.

The GT350R enjoyed a loyal following and great success, thanks in part to it exclusivity. It was sold as a special model available through a limited number of dealers.B
DescriptionLong.0x0000515A:
Not many car makers in the world can compete with Radical Sportscars Ltd. when it comes to creating pure unbridled performance cars. Since 1970, when the company was founded, Radical has been providing lightweight mid-engine race cars, powered by high-performance motorcycle engines, to the motorsports public. The vehicles were so popular that Radical began producing road-going versions that slightly resembled Le Mans prototype race cars.

The idea behind the road-going car was that anyone could drive it from his or her own home to the race track, then drive it back home, without the need for a trailer or car transporter. Of all the Radicals offered, the SR3 SL was the most gentlemanly. No major changes were made to its design principles and styling, but the car did come equipped with an automobile engine to meet the variety of emissions regulations around the world. The power unit was a Ford Ecoboost direct-injection turbocharged 2.0 liter inline-4 that produced <240ps> in standard form, with an option to go up to <300ps>. The gearbox was a 6-speed sequential unit with paddle shifters.

The lightweight <775kg> car went from zero to <96km/h> in 3.4 seconds and peaked at <257km/h>. The SR3 SL came to a full stop from <96km/h> in just 2.67 seconds. The SR3 SL’s performance was leaps and bounds beyond the norm, making it the quintessential road-going race car.
DescriptionLong.0x0000515B:
The Ferrari Testarossa (Type F110) was introduced as the company's mid-engine flagship in 1984, replacing the popular 512BB in the lineup. Penned by Pininfarina, the car boasted a wild exterior design that was highlighted by its signature side strakes. 

At first glance, the strakes may appear to be just a wild design element, but in reality, they directed air to the car's Formula 1-style radiators. The cooling air was necessary to keep the car's 5.0-liter 180-degree V-12 running smooth. This mid-mounted engine produced <390ps> and <50.0kgm> of torque, allowing the car to run from zero to <100km/h> in just 5.8 seconds and reach a top speed of <290km/h>.

Production of the Testarossa, which translated to "red head" in Italian, halted in 1992, making the way for the 512 TR.
DescriptionLong.0x0000515C:
The SUV genre may well have started with this vehicle, a compact 4-wheel-drive off-roader that was commissioned by the United States Army for use during World War II. 

The United States asked Bantam, Ford and Willys to develop and produce prototypes of all-terrain vehicles based on a design by Bantam. Each company built more than 1500 examples that were immediately put to use on the battlefront. Here, the Willys MA shined the brightest, so the U.S. Army placed its order and Willy delivered the MB, of which 360,000 units were eventually manufactured. 

When the war ended, Willys registered the Jeep trademark and offered a production-based MB for the general public. Because of its success and exposure during the war, it was an instant hit, thus the SUV was born and the MB's place in the annals of automotive history solidified.
DescriptionLong.0x0000529D:
In 2016, the 1951 Ford Custom Club Coupe drove away with the coveted Gran Turismo Award, a prize presented every year at the SEMA show in Las Vegas to the best customized car at the convention. 

This particular example was built by a team of specialists working for former racing driver Bruce Leven, who incorporated Leven's vision of a classic racing Ford with elements of European style; thus, the Custom Club Coupe features major bodywork that includes a slimmer waistline and lower roof. 

Under the hood of this mean machine is a 1956 Lincoln 368 cu.-in. V-8 tuned to produce <380ps>. Chassis enhancements included the front and rear suspension constructed to provide competition spec handling. Nearly every piece of this car was customized, with the team saying it took an estimated 10,000 hours of work to complete the entire vehicle.
DescriptionLong.0x0000529E:
The Cappuccino was an instant hit when it was introduced by Suzuki in November 1991. Along with the other sporty kei-cars such as the Honda Beat and Mazda Autozam AZ-1, the Cappuccino provided unprecedented flair to the mainly economy-oriented kei-car category.

Like a traditional sport car, the Cappuccino adopted a 2-seat front-engine/rear-wheel-drive layout in a convertible body. In contrast, the Beat and the gull-winged AZ-1 featured mid-engine layouts. And although kei-cars often shared parts, the Cappuccino had an all-original body. Suzuki ensured that it was a capable handling machine, giving it a 51:49 front-to-rear weight distribution and a sport-tuned suspension system consisting of double wishbones at front and rear. 

Another innovative element of the Cappuccino was its three-piece detachable roof. With all the pieces in place, the car was essentially a hard-top coupe, but depending on how you configured them, the car could be converted to a T-top, a targa-top or a full-on convertible, offering the owner four different body styles.

Under the hood was a <657cc> turbocharged DOHC 12-valve inline-3 based on the <64ps> powerplant of the Alto Works, the most powerful engine used in a kei model. Providing stopping power were disc brakes at all four corners with ventilated front discs. 

In 1995, the car received a number of minor improvements including an a newly designed all-aluminum engine block. The engine control unit was also updated. An electronically controlled 3-speed automatic joined the 5-speed manual gearbox in the lineup, with the automatic transmission models equipped with power steering.

At the end of 1998, the production run for the Cappuccino ended at 26,500 units, but the car remains popular today with collectors and driving enthusiasts, and is still considered one of the greatest kei-cars of all time.
DescriptionLong.0x0000529F:
In 1973, Caterham Cars secured the rights to manufacture the open-cockpit sports and race car called the Seven from Lotus Cars. In 1996, Caterham Cars decided to take the car's performance to another level with the Seven Superlight.

This new version of the British classic came with a semi-monocoque chassis built from a tubular frame with aluminum paneling. semi-monocoque chassis built from a tubular frame with aluminum paneling.
While it possessed the basic visual cues of the original Seven, the Superlight weighed significantly less than the stock version, from <35kg> to <50kg> less depending on the engine you chose.

The "R500" version of this car was introduced in 1999. Its name was derived from the car's 500-horsepower-per-ton power-to-weight ratio.  The first vehicles were equipped with a Rover K-series engine, but in 2008, Caterham decided to throw a <266ps> 2.0-liter Ford Duratec under the hood, giving the R500 supercar-like acceleration: Its zero to <100km/h> came in at 2.88 seconds and top speed was rated at 150 mph.
DescriptionLong.0x000052A0:
Introduced as a 1964 model, the Chevelle was Chevrolet's first mid-size model. With an SS sports variant in the lineup, and an option for a 327 cu.-in. high-output V-8 engine, the Chevelle possessed all the hallmarks of a muscle car.

In 1965, the Chevelle SS was transformed into a full-blown high-performance car, equipped with a 396 cu.-in. OHV V-8. From then on, the Chevelle SS was only offered with this 396 cu.-in. unit, drawing a clear line between it and the previous SS.

In 1970, the Chevelle SS was called the most powerful mid-size car in the marketplace. The base engine had been upgraded to 402 cu. in., and the higher grade 427 cu. in. engine was upgraded to 454 cu. in.

The codenames for the two 454 cu.-in.-equipped models were the LS5 and LS6. The former produced <360ps>, with a compression ratio of 10.25:1. The latter doled out approximately <456ps>, with an increased compression ratio of 11.25:1. It also came with high cams and high-flow headers. This was the most powerful production-model engine in the history of American cars at the time.

The LS6-equipped Chevelle SS 454 was immediately recognized as a very special model, with its high power output that surpassed many road-legal cars. Equipped with a straight exhaust and carburetor settings, it was said to have easily exceeded <500ps> and became a force in stock class drag races.
DescriptionLong.0x000052A1:
When you talk about hot Honda Civics, surely the 6th iteration of this compact-car icon that first appeared in 1972 would take the forefront of the conversation. The car known in-house as the "EK" and dubbed by Civic loyalists as the "Miracle Civic" arrived in 1995. It boasted excellent fuel economy, high output three-stage VTEC, and a CVT (Continuously Variable Transmission) called the Honda Multimatic.

It came in 3-door hatchback and sedan forms, the latter called the Ferio in Japan. This Civic won Japan's prestigious Car of the Year award, as well as racking up a number of different honors all over the world. In August 1997, Honda introduced a "Type R" variant, which was based on the Civic hatchback. It was the first "Type R" model in Civic's history.

The engine of the Civic Type R was a B16B, a 1.6-liter DOHC 16-valve inline-4, equipped with VTEC. The engine cranked out an amazing <185ps>/<8200rpm>, figures previously unheard of in a naturally aspirated engine. Also, it was lighter than the other Civics, making it that much quicker off the line.

The car was also an excellent handling machine thanks to a lowered body and firmer suspension. Naturally, the Type R made for an exceptional racer, with many victories in Grassroots Motorsports and in Japan's Super Taikyu endurance series. Even after all these years, the car still has a loyal following.
DescriptionLong.0x000052A2:
A full model change in the autumn of 1967 introduced the new C3 Corvette Stingray as a 1968 model. It was very reminiscent of the Mako Shark II show car, which was shown at the New York International Auto Show in April 1965.

This concept sought to show off the Corvette in a new light, specifically as a grand tourer. Chief designer Bill Mitchell's design ideas were extremely important factors in the achievement of this goal.

Working as Mitchell's right-hand man was a man named Larry Shinoda, a Japanese-American who had worked as a detail designer on the original Stingray. Taking many hints from Mitchell's concepts, Shinoda's image of the next-generation GT car materialized in the form of the Mako Shark II.

With a dynamic, curvaceous exterior, and an interior stuffed with the newest electronic gizmos, it was indeed the Corvette of the future. The essence of this idea was thoroughly incorporated into the street model that was to become the C3 Corvette.

In 1969 the standard engine's displacement was increased from 327 cu. in. to 350 cu. in., but maximum output remained unchanged at <300ps>. At the same time, the small-block option changed from the 327 cu.-in. L79 to the 350 cu.-in. L46, with maximum output again unchanged at <355ps>.

Although at the time, there was mention of a big-block Corvette, the small-block engine held the advantage in handling with its lower frontal weight. The epitome of this was the replacement of the top-grade L46 by the <370ps> LT1. Available around 1970, this was acclaimed as the best handling of all the C3 Corvette combinations.
DescriptionLong.0x000052A3:
When it comes to custom cars, the U.S. ranks number one in terms of quality, volume and genre. And, by far, the oldest genre—one that is now an iconic part of American culture—is the hot rod. This was a movement that originated in the 1930s, where the Ford Model T, and later the Model A and Model B, were heavily modified by their owners. Extensive exterior modifications were performed on these cars, such as removing fenders and engine hoods, and altering the body to make chop-tops. Later, as newer and more powerful engines were developed elsewhere in the world, they then were mounted into these vehicles.

The most well-known platform for this practice was the Ford Model B. Why? Not just because it was the first car of the era to be powered by a V8, it was also quite rare—the Model B was only produced for a single year, in 1932.

The vehicle with number plate "V-3883" displayed in the Henry Ford Museum is one such car based on the Model B, carrying the nickname of "Deuce." It was built by Richard Smith of Phoenix, Arizona, in 1954, with US $2800 (a considerable sum back then) and a massive amount of time and effort. The V-3883 is a classic "highboy" style hot rod, with removed fenders, but the engine has been swapped for a <180ps> Chrysler 331 Hemi. The side panels have been cut and modified to accommodate the wide engine, and the engine covers are now part of the exterior accents. This is a car that has been crafted to the very last detail; it is a simple, yet beautiful example of the "good old days."F
DescriptionLong.0x000052A4:
The "baby" Lamborghini, officially known as the Gallardo, was introduced in 2003. Since then, the car has evolved over the years, with performance enhancements as well as additional higher-performance models added to the lineup.

The most notable of these appeared at the 2008 Geneva Motor Show as the Gallardo LP 560-4. Upon first glance, the car's aggressive styling seemed to be influenced by the limited-edition (and very expensive) Lamborghini Reventón, making it one of the meanest looking cars to wear the charging bull badge.

As for the car's performance... it was equally mean. The most prominent change under the sheet metal was the engine, a V-10 that grew from <4961cc> to <5204cc>. Breathing improvements were also performed and, when combined with its higher compression ratio, the engine produced a whopping <560ps> and <55.1kgm> of torque, an improvement of <40ps> and <3.1kgm> from the original Gallardo's powerplant. Power was routed to all four wheels (the "560" in the car's name is a reference to engine output, while the "4" stood for 4WD).

A choice of two transmissions came mated to the engine, both inherited from the previous model, a 6-speed manual or the semi-automatic 6-speed gearbox called E-gear, the latter featuring shifts that were 40 percent faster than the human hand when set to "CORSA" mode.

Weight of the LP 560-4 was trimmed by <20kg> from the previous model to <1410kg>, which helped the car reach a top speed of <325km/h> and blast from zero to <100km/h> in 3.7 seconds.-
DescriptionLong.0x000052A5:
The Honda Integra was sold as the Acura Integra in the US.

People didn't call the third-generation Acura Integra the "100 meter eye catcher" for no reason. This term meant that it was instantly recognizable from as far away as 100 meters, a testament to the car’s unusual four round headlights. The new-look Integra proved to be a hit in the U.S. when it arrived in May 1993, but it proved too radical for the Japanese public. So in response to its less-than-stellar sales in Japan, the Japan-market version returned to more conventional-looking trapezoidal headlights two years later.

The second most noteworthy thing about the new Integra was the inclusion of a Type R model. By this time, sports car enthusiasts were already familiar with the "Type R" moniker, thanks to the emergence of the NSX Type R in 1992. In the Integra's case, the engine was based on the Si's 1.8-liter VTEC B18. This high-compression motor featured high-pressure piston heads, special control rods and two-fold valve springs. Each component of this inline-4 was meticulously tuned, resulting in <200ps>, or <111ps> per liter. Honda chassis engineers refortified the Integra's chassis, at the same time making it lighter by removing sound insulation and installing a smaller battery. Switching to lightweight aluminum wheels also shaved off <40kg>. The Type R became the poster child for the ultimate front-wheel-drive sports machine, and spurned the 98spec. R in 1998 that came with equal-length exhausts and 16-in. wheels.
DescriptionLong.0x000052A6:
The Maserati Merak, a mid-engine sports car introduced in 1972, was developed as a sister model to the Bora that came out the previous year. Both vehicles shared the same basic exterior styling, penned by renown designer Giugiaro; however, the rear ends were noticeably different, as the Bora was a fastback, while the Merak was a notchback with a fastback-style pillar. 

The engines of the two cars were also different. Where the Bora had a rumbling V-8 in its engine bay, the Merak featured a <190ps> 3.0-liter V-6 borrowed from the Citroën SM, thus allowing the Merak to adopt a 2+2 layout and boast more luggage space. 

In 1975, a high-performance version of the Merak was offered, called the Merak SS, which came equipped with a <220ps> engine that increased the car's top speed from <225km/h> to <250km/h>.F
DescriptionLong.0x000052A7:
The R8 was originally a Le Mans Prototype race car. Its name and much of its technology were incorporated into a road-going version of the car, which made its debut in 2006. The R8 road car met with worldwide critical acclaim, prompting the arrival of a second-generation model in 2016.

The new R8 adopted the original car's basic formula, but there were key changes, including a new version of the lightweight Audi Space Frame constructed from lightweight materials. It also had an updated version of the quattro AWD system. While the new car's exterior styling appeared similar to that of its predecessor, most of its details here were completely new.

Inside the engine bay was the same 5.2-liter V-10 as before, but the one in the second-generation R8 produced <15ps> more, bringing total output to <540ps>. Also, the new model lineup featured the "R8 V10 Plus," which increased power to <610ps>, while adding a fixed rear wing and mechanical LSD as standard fare. The newly tuned engine allowed the R8 V10 Plus to run from zero to <100km> in a scant 3.2 seconds and reach a top speed of <330km/h>.
DescriptionLong.0x000052A8:
From the middle of the 1969 season, the Charger 500 Daytona made its appearance in stock car racing. It took full advantage of its aerodynamics, and was performing very well. This in turn raised demand from teams racing Plymouth race cars which are in the same Chrysler group, for a model that has the same aerodynamics as the Daytona.

The answer to those demands was the Superbird.

Because Plymouth did not produce a vehicle that could be considered the sibling of the Charger, the Road Runner — with the same intermediate-class chassis — was selected to be its base.

Because of the familiar extended nose and rear wing, it looks very similar to the Daytona, but there are slight differences to details such as the shape of the roof.

Because the number of cars required for homologation was doubled in 1970 from 500 cars to 1000, and with the Daytona’s performing so well on the circuit, many Superbirds made it to the streets, not just the circuit.

The base engine for the Superbird was the <375ps> 440 Super Commando, with a 426 Hemi producing over <425ps>, and a <390ps> 440 six barrel as options. This was more in line with the GTX, which was ranked above the Road Runner.

The Superbird was produced, like the Daytona, during the homologation certification period of only one year.
DescriptionLong.0x000052A9:
The FD3S, the third-generation RX-7, made its debut in December 1991. The “Savanna” name used on earlier versions was retired, and the model was rebadged as the ɛ̃fini RX-7.

To accommodate wider tires, the FD3S was significantly widened. Even so, extensive use of aluminum for the hood, spare wheel, jack, and front and rear double-wishbone suspension kept curb weight to a remarkable <1260kg>, despite the increase in size.

Power came from the 13B Turbo carried over from the FC3S. But the addition of a new sequential twin-turbo system raised output to <255ps> and <30.0kgm> of torque. In its lighter Type S form, the power-to-weight ratio reached <4.90kg/ps>, making it the fastest RX-7 ever released and a platform with enormous potential.

The FD3S continued to evolve throughout its lifecycle. Body rigidity, engine management, and ABS specifications were refined year after year. The original Type I introduced in 1991 progressed through Type II and Type III, culminating in the Type VI released in 2000.

Ultimately, the RX-7 could not meet the tightening environmental standards of the 21st century. In August 2002, the RX-7 Spirit R was released as a final commemorative model, closing the book on 25 years of RX-7 production.
DescriptionLong.0x00005550:
De Tomaso introduced its second production sports car, the mid-engine Mangusta, in 1966, after its first offering, the Vallelunga, left many serious drivers wanting for more power. So, instead of going with the Vallelunga's 1.5-liter inline-4, De Tomaso chose to install a Ford V-8 into the new car. North American Mangustas received the 302-cu.-in. engine while other models took on the 289-cu.in. version. Both versions produced <310ps> and were mated to a ZF-made 5-speed gearbox. 

The car was extremely lightweight, weighing in at a lean <1300kg>, which allowed the Mangusta to run to <100km> in 6.0 seconds and reach a top speed of <250km/h>. 

Although only 401 were made, the combination of the gorgeous Italian bodywork designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro, who was working for Carrozzeria Ghia at the time, and American V-8 power set the stage for the famous De Tomaso Pantera that came along in 1970.
DescriptionLong.0x00005551:
The Nissan GT-R GT3, based on the road-going R35 GT-R, was a familiar presence in the FIA's GT3 class. When the race car was introduced in 2012, it came powered by the same twin-turbo 3.8-liter V-6 as in the production model, with the output of the engine rated well above <500ps>.

A new version of the race car appeared in 2015 with a stiffer body structure and going by a new name: the Nismo GT3. In 2018, a dry sump oil system was incorporated to allow the powerplant to sit lower in the engine bay by <150mm>, giving the car a better overall center of gravity. It was also moved aft by <150mm> to optimize front and rear weight distribution. 

The radiators and intercoolers were repositioned to provide enhanced airflow and better engine cooling. By redirecting how the air flowed over the body, the Nismo GT3 possessed improved body stability, while a stiffer front body rigidity and retuned suspension system improved handling.
DescriptionLong.0x0000565B:
Introduced by Porsche in 2011, the 918 Spyder succeeded the Carrera GT as the company's flagship model and was its first road-going supercar to feature a hybrid powerplant.  

Based on the powertrain of the RS Spyder prototype race car, the 918 Spyder's drive system takes a <608ps> 4.6-liter V-8, mounted amidships, and mates it with a single electric motor at the rear. The combined output totals a whopping <886p>, enabling the 918 to reach <100km/h> in just 2.6 seconds, <200km/h> in 7.2 and <300km/h> in just 19.9, when equipped with the Weissach Package that reduces the car’s curb weight from <1674kg> to <1634kg>. 

The 918 Spyder, of which only 918 examples were made, claimed a top speed of <345km/h> and lapped the famed Nürburgring Nordschleife in 6 minutes and 57 seconds.
DescriptionLong.0x0000565C:
BMW followed up its popular 2800 CS, introduced in 1968, with the 3.0 CS luxury sports coupe three years later. 

The 2800 CS wore the body of the 1965 2000 C, but possessed a longer front overhang to make room for a 2.8-liter inline-6, replacing the 2000C's four-cylinder engine. With the 3.0 CS, BMW enlarged the engine, known as the "Big Six," to 3.0 liters, resulting in <180ps> and <26.0kgm> of torque. To offset the power increase, BMW fitted 4-wheel disc brakes to the 3.0 CS.

Such a car would make for an excellent race car, BMW concluded, so when the 3.0 CS took to the track, a special lightweight homologation version was offered, one that weighed <200kg> less than the base model. This car was called the 3.0 CSL with the "L" standing for "leicht," which means lightweight in German.
DescriptionLong.0x0000565D:
It wasn't until 1953 until America produced its first real sports car. Until then, U.S. roads were replete with stylish, nimble European sports cars imported en masse after World War II. But everything changed when General Motors produced the Chevrolet Corvette.  

The new American sports car boasted cutting-edge technology, including fiberglass body panels and a steel backbone frame. It was powerful too, equipped with a <152ps> 3.8-liter inline-6 mounted in the <4249mm> long, <1773mm> wide body. All 1953 Vettes were handmade and only 300 examples were produced. 

When this first batch sold out almost instantly, GM set up a new factory in St. Louis the following year to meet demand. As a result, 3,640 Corvettes went into customers' hands that year, 10 times more than the previous year. 

While the 1954 model was essentially the same as the original, midway through the model year, the cam profile was changed, and engine output increased to <155ps>. In 1958, the Corvette had its first significant facelift, highlighted by a four-headlight front end.
DescriptionLong.0x0000565F:
In 2020, special editions of the Alfa Romeo Giulia were introduced to celebrate the 110th anniversary of the historic company. The cars were called the Giulia GTA and GTAm, which were based on the high-performance Quadrifoglio model.

For these cars, the power output of the twin-turbocharged 2.9-liter V-6 was increased to <540ps>, while curb weight was reduced by <100kg>. Also, the front and rear track were widened by <50mm> to enhance the car's stability, while the cars' aerodynamics were significantly enhanced in the form of new front and rear fenders, as well as other redeisgned body parts, thanks to help from Alfa Romeo's Formula 1 partner, Sauber.

The GTAm offers a more hardcore setup designed for circuit use. In addition to a larger front splitter and carbon fiber rear wing, a roll-cage was installed and the rear seats were removed.
DescriptionLong.0x00005660:
The first BMW M3 appeared in 1985, and it represented a high-performance version of the popular 3 Series (E30) that could also be used for touring car racing.

At first, the M3 only came in 2-door form, with wider treads and sporty fender flares. Also, front and rear spoilers were added, aggressive side skirts were installed and the angle of the C-pillar and rear window were revised to create a car that looked much meaner than the stock 3 Series. These body modifications also resulted in a better Cd of 0.38 (from 0.33). Under the hood was a special 2.3-liter DOHC inline-4 that produced <195ps> and <23.4kgm> of torque.

The race-spec model was introduced in 1987. From the onset, it dominated the DTM, winning five of the first 10 races. That same year, the M3 Evolution was released with even better aerodynamics and a <210ps> engine. In 1988, output was increased to <220ps> for the M3 Evolution II. In 1989 the final model of the E30 M3, called the M3 Sports Evolution, appeared, equipped with a larger engine (2.5 liters) that produced <238ps>/<24.5kgm>.
DescriptionLong.0x00005661:
Mercedes-Benz introduced an AMG version of the fourth-generation C-Class a year after the base model was introduced in 2014. And although it wore the same C63 badge as its predecessor, the 2015 AMG C63 featured an all-new powerplant. Gone was the naturally aspirated 6.2-liter V-8, replaced by a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8 known as the M177, which used the same basic configuration as the M178 in the AMG GT.

The new C63 delivered <476ps> and <66.3kgm> in base form, and the C63 S provided a whopping <510ps> and <71.4kgm>. While horsepower was the same as the AMG GT models, the C63 engine featured better torque delivery that came lower in the rpm spectrum. Because of this, the C63 behaved in a smooth, civil manner on public roads. Only after the sedan and station wagon body styles were introduced did Mercedes-Benz offer the C63 and C63 S as a coupe in 2016.
DescriptionLong.0x00005663:
The Swift has traditionally been one of Suzuki's most popular models, especially the Swift Sport, which has been touted as one of the most fun-to-drive compact sports coupes in Japan. When the fourth-generation Swift was introduced in 2016, the Swift Sport wasn't far behind, coming out a year later.

With a lower front end that enhanced the car's aerodynamics, the new Swift Sport wasn't simply better looking, but a better performer in every way. Under the hood was a turbocharged 1.4-liter engine that replaced the previous model's naturally aspirated 1.6-liter, putting out a respectable <140ps> and 230 Nm (<23.45 kgm>). 

Also, because Suzuki engineers retuned the car's suspension system, while also widening the front and rear track by 30mm, the car handled better than ever. The car was <70kg> lighter than before, so it possessed a pronounced low- and mid-range punch.
DescriptionLong.0x00005676:
As a stunning new take on a legendary racing car, the new Ford GT supercar was launched in the summer of 2004 to commemorate the company's 100th anniversary. As a reinterpretation of the classic 1960s GT40 that won four straight 24 Hours of Le Mans races, this new version featured the latest and greatest automotive technology. With that in mind, Grand Turismo decided to make a good thing even better by creating its own Ford GT to contemporary Le Mans specs, we call it the Ford GT LM Race Car.

The powertrain remains the same as that found in the production Ford GT, a supercharged 5.4-liter DOHC V8 mounted amidships behind the seats. But the <558ps> output from the stock version has been boosted to a whopping <600ps> in this race car model. A 6-speed manual race-spec gearbox has also been added.

The LM Race Car has the identical proportions as that of the stock Ford GT, measuring <4.61m> from bumper to bumper and <1.95m> wide. The chassis is an aluminum space frame design incorporating all of the latest automotive technologies, and the body is composed entirely of carbon-fiber. A large rear wing for increased downforce has also been added. The suspension system consists of a double-wishbone configuration fore and aft. Total curb weight: just <1150kg>.'
DescriptionLong.0x000057E8:
One of the most storied sports cars in history is the Porsche 911, and among the most popular versions of this classic German sports car is the Type 964, the third-generation model introduced in 1989. While its exterior appeared nearly identical to its predecessor, the 930, the 964 featured approximately 80 percent of new parts, all but making it an all-new model.  

The 964 was offered in three different trim levels: the rear-drive Carrera 2 base car, the all-wheel-drive Carrera 4 and the high-performance 911 Turbo. When the 911 Turbo made its debut, it came with the same turbocharged 3.3-liter flat-6 in the Type 930 911 Turbo, producing <320ps>, but in 1993, Porsche upgraded the powerplant to a turbocharged 3.6-liter, increasing power to <360ps>. The new 911 Turbo 3.6 looked meaner too, with a body lowered by <20mm>, the addition of Speedline 18-inch wheels and a special RS bumper.

The Type 964 remains one of the most popular 911 models ever, and the 964 911 Turbo has become a highly sought-after car for classic Porsche collectors everywhere.
DescriptionLong.0x000057E9:
Many race aficionados know that Alpine is a revered marque in the rallying world, as the A110 remains one of the most successful rally cars in history. That said, the French automaker also carved out a niche on the tarmac with a series of successful prototype race cars in the 1960s, among them being the M63 (1963) and the M64, which was followed by the M65 in 1965. The M cars were succeeded by the A210, introduced in 1966, which went on to take the top three spots of the energy efficiency index of the 1967 24 Hours of Le Mans.  

While the A210 managed to take a few class victories in various races in 1967, Alpine wanted the overall title at the 1968 24 Hours of Le Mans, so it went to work on a machine that could accomplish this feat. The result was the A220 that came powered by a new 3.0-liter V-8 that produced <300ps> and weighed <80kg> less than the A210. While it was decidedly quicker than the A210, the A220 failed to meet Alpine's lofty goals, but it remains as one of the most loved models of Alpine today because it was the final race car built exclusively by the company before it became part of the Renault Group.
DescriptionLong.0x000057EA:
In 2017, Honda took its rich history in racing and incorporated it into its popular compact sports coupe, the Civic Type R. Unlike Civic Type Rs before it, this fifth-generation model was not merely an upgraded version of the base Civic, but a car that had been developed from the ground up as a pure Type R performance machine.

The new Civic Type R's turbocharged, direct-injected 2.0-liter inline-4 was carried over from the previous model with power increased by <10ps> to <320ps>, thanks to the fine tuning of the engine control system. The front suspension was totally redesigned, while the rear multilink setup was significantly stiffened. All of these changes resulted in a car that set the fastest FWD lap time at the Nürburgring with a blistering time of 7 minutes 43.80 seconds.

The 2020 model took things a step further with the addition of special forged wheels and a lighter curb weight by <20lb>. With a limited production run of 1000 units, the 2020 Civic Type R sold out in a matter of minutes.L
DescriptionLong.0x000057EB:
Ferrari introduced the F8 Tribute in 2019 to succeed the 488GTB. While the silhouettes of the two cars were quite similar, they exuded a different ambience altogether. 

The F8 Tribute was essentially an update of the 488GTB; therefore, the engine, which was mounted amidships, was carried over from the 488 Pista. This powerplant was a twin-turbocharged 3.9-liter V-8 that produced <720ps> and <78.5kgm> of torque. For the exterior, the body was slightly restyled to improve aerodynamics and redirect air flow to optimize engine cooling. Inside the cockpit, the dashboard, instrument cluster, and door panels were replaced to give the car a fresh look and feel for the driver.

The performance of the F8 Tribute was nominally better than its predecessor with a 0-<100km/h> time of 2.9 seconds, a 0-<200km/h> time of 7.8 and a top speed of <340km/h>.
DescriptionLong.0x000057EC:
As far as rally-inspired performance sedans go, Mitsubishi's Lancer Evolution VII, introduced in 2001, was in a class of its own, one-upping its main rival, the Subaru WRX STI. The new Evo featured cutting-edge all-wheel-drive technologies that included the ACD (Active Center Differential) and the AYC yaw-control system. In 2002, Mitsubishi offered an INVECS-II electronically controlled automatic transmission with manual shift mode, mating it with a detuned <272ps> version of the 4G63 engine. 

In 2003, Mitsubishi introduced the Lancer Evolution VIII whose engine produced <40kgm> more torque than its predecessor, along with enhancements to the drivetrain and handling components. This set the stage for the Lancer Evolution VIII MR, which made its debut in 2004. As the final Evo VIII model, the MR came with various refinements across the board, including the addition of an aluminum roof panel and the implementation of Bilstein dampers for the very first time.
DescriptionLong.0x000057ED:
Many motorsports historians consider the McLaren MP4/4 as the most successful race cars ever built. This machine, designed by Gordon Murray and Steve Nichols and powered by the Honda RA168E engine, dominated the 1988 Formula 1 World Championship season, winning all but one race (15 out of 16 races) and taking all but one pole position.

Much of the credit was attributed to the Honda engine that effectively balanced fuel consumption and raw power, but the chassis was also superior to the rest of the field. Another big factor was the driving team of Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost, who helped score McLaren-Honda a then-record 199 points in the Constructors Championship. Senna took the drivers' title that year although Prost scored more points. The reason was that only the eleven best results counted, and Senna had more first-place finishes than Prost (eight to seven).
DescriptionLong.0x000057EF:
Ruf continues to create distinctive sports cars, all of them based on Porsche models, and infusing them with its own unique philosophy and craftsmanship. Among their enduring model lines is the “RGT,” based on 911 GT3 models.

At the heart of the RGT lies the concept of enhancing the performance of the GT3 while endowing it with the comfort of a road car. At the 2015 Geneva show, Ruf unveiled a new addition to this lineage: the RGT 4.2, based on the Type 991, 911 GT3.

As its name suggested, it came powered by a 4.2-liter flat-6 engine, increasing the displacement from the standard 3.8 liters of the Type 991, 911 GT3 by nearly <400cc>. However, the increased displacement was not its only notable feature. It employed the renowned “Mezger" touch with the GT1 crankshaft at its foundation—an engine celebrated for its racing success since the days of the air-cooled flat-6. The car produced an impressive <125ps> per liter, culminating in a maximum power output of <525ps>.

In terms of design, the RGT 4.2 boasted aggressive riveted overfenders, while the interior featured an integrated roll cage, an element for which the RGT series is renowned. Combining the spirit of competition with the elegance of a road car, this model exemplified the Ruf ethos, offering the ultimate vehicle for the gentleman driver who sought both track performance and daily usability.
DescriptionLong.0x000057F0:
Produced from 1927 to 1933, the Model S is considered the first sports car produced by Mercedes Benz. Designed by Dr. Ferdinand Porsche, the Model S chassis boasted much improved performance than that of its predecessor, the Model K. Powering the car was a supercharged 7.0-liter inline-6 that produced <180ps>, which was quite high in its day. 

This Model S shown here won the Best of Show and the Gran Turismo Trophy at the 2017 Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance. Nicknamed the "Barker Tourer," this car was a one-off and remains very valuable. It was first owned by Earl Howe, a decorated racing driver who won both the Mille Miglia and the 24 Hours of Le Mans and was a co-founder of the British Racing Driver’s Club. He commissioned Barker, a British coachbuilder founded in 1710, to build him a lightweight tourer body with a boat-tail design, and the company delivered him the beauty you see here.
DescriptionLong.0x000057F1:
The 550/1500RS was a purpose-built racing sports car that Porsche introduced in late 1954.

Its name, “550,” reflected its impressively light dry weight of just <550kg>. Built on a steel tube frame clad in an aluminum body, the car was powered by a 4-cam flat-four engine that produced <135ps>.

The 550/1500RS quickly proved itself on the racing circuit, capturing its class win at the 1954 24 Hours of Le Mans. The following year, it finished 4th overall, repeating its class victory.

One notable example was chassis number 550-0067, finished in French Blue. Delivered originally to a French dealership, this car also made an appearance at the Paris Motor Show.

This extremely historic race car still wears its original livery from its participation in the 1956 24 Hours of Le Mans race and is said to have been owned by famed French race driver Jean Marie Behra.
DescriptionLong.0x00007F6B:
One of the most notable versions of the 350Z (Z33) was the Version NISMO Type 380RS. Created by the motorsports arm of Nissan, the NISMO 380RS possessed many technologies that were developed for the race track.

With only 300 units produced, the 380RS featured a stiffer body structure than the base car, reinforced brakes, tuned suspension, front and rear aerodynamic bumpers and a new rear spoiler. Under the hood was a VQ35HR 3.8-liter V-6 that was detuned for road use. Output was rated at <350ps> at <7200rpm> and <40.5kgm> of torque that peaked at <4800rpm>.

Tuning firm Power House Amuse took this car and worked its own magic on it. Called the Amuse NISMO 380RS Super Leggera, the car had a different compression ratio and upgraded intake and exhaust systems that resulted in <386ps> and <41.8kgm> of torque. Also, as its name implies, curb weight was reduced by <140kg> by extensive use of carbon fiber and titanium. 

This car made its public debut at the 2008 Tokyo Auto Salon where it received the Gran Turismo Award.
DescriptionLong.0x00007F6C:
The sixth-generation Toyota Celica, introduced in October 1993, solidified the model's image as one of the world's most popular front-wheel-drive sports coupes. The styling direction of the new model took a wild turn for the better, highlighted by a svelte roofline and a distinctive front fascia that featured four round headlights. 

The car was powered by either the 3S-GE, a <185ps> 2.0-liter DOHC inline-4 in the SS-II model, or the 3S-FE that produced <140ps> in the SS-I. The suspension system consisted of struts all around and disc brakes at all four corners. 

In February 1994, Toyota introduced the Celica GT-Four to serve as a base for its World Rally Championship race car. The GT-Four is now known as the ultimate performance Celica, equipped with aluminum hood and a rear spoiler, with a powerful <225ps> 3S-GTE turbocharged 2.0-liter powerplant. *
DescriptionLong.0x00007F6D:
The third-generation Dodge Challenger, introduced in 2008 as the true successor to the Challenger muscle car, is known for its various high-performance variants, but the one that stood out was the most powerful version, the SRT Hellcat that made its debut in 2015.  

But in 2018. the Hellcat was upstaged by an even more sinister model, the SRT Demon of which only 3,300 units were produced.

This car was developed for the single purpose of winning drag races. The engine, based on the one in the Hellcat, was tuned to produce <852ps> on 100 or higher-octane fuel. This allowed the car to boast a zero to 62 mph time of 2.3 seconds and reach the quarter-mile mark of just 9.65. The body featured a full drag-strip setup with no passenger or rear seats included as standard equipment, although they are available as an option. 

Adding even more spice to the package was the "Demon Crate," a race parts kit that Dodge sold to buyers for just one dollar extra. The equipment, said to be valued at more than US $6000, included thinner front wheels, a high-octane-tuned ECU for drag racing, air filters and a race-spec instrument panel.

The SRT Demon was banned from racing in stock form by the NHRA (National Hot Rod Association), which said the car was too fast to compete without a roll cage or parachute. The Demon is certain to go down in Dodge history as one of the greatest monsters the company ever produced.
DescriptionLong.0x00007F6E:
Since its introduction in 2012, more than 200,000 units of the Toyota 86 were sold around the world, solidifying its place in the history books as one of the most popular front-engine/rear-wheel-drive compact sports cars of all time.

Nine years after the 86's debut, Toyota introduced the GR86, a high-performance version of the car that wore the Gazoo Racing badge (GR). While maintaining the virtues of the original car, namely a lightweight body and superb handling, Toyota engineers equipped the GR86 with a larger engine. Under the bonnet was a 2.4-litre flat-4 that replaced the 2.0-litre variant. Power came in at an impressive <235ps>/<7000rpm> with maximum torque peaking at <25.5kgm>/<3700rpm>. This translated to a 0-<100km/h> acceleration time of 6.3 seconds, which was a stark improvement over the 7.4 seconds of the first-generation model.

To enhance the 86's handling, the company's chassis engineers stiffened the body and adopted aluminium in the roof panel to lower the center of gravity, as well as reduce overall weight. With the GR86, Toyota offered sports-car enthusiasts exactly what they were hoping for with the 86: a meaner, faster version of the car that was designed for the race track.
DescriptionLong.0x00007F6F:
Since its debut in 2014, the Mercedes-AMG GT came in various forms, including a roadster and a 4-door coupe. There were high-performance versions offered, including the potent AMG GT Black Series that was introduced in 2020. 

The Black Series represented the pinnacle of the AMG performance brand, thus, the AMG GT Black Series possessed true race car technology. Under its hood was a specially tuned twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8 that produced <730ps> and 800 Nm (<81.57kgm>) of torque. It came mated to a strengthen 7-speed DCT transmission whose gear ratios were revised. The end result was a car that ran from zero to <100km/h> in 3.2 seconds, to <200km/h> within 9 seconds and reach a top speed of <325km/h>.

Not all about going fast in the straight line, AMG tuned the chassis to capably handle the extra power, while the body was reshaped in various places to provide adequate downforce. In short, the AMG GT Black Series is a race car for the street, tuned to the nth degree by the most prominent luxury and motorsports brand in the world.
DescriptionLong.0x00007F70:
The Ford Mustang has always included high-performance versions in its lineup with many examples created especially for racing. 

One of the first special Mustang versions to be specifically used in motorsports was the GT350, developed by Shelby American for SCCA races. Then, there was the BOSS series, produced in 1969 and 1970, a high-performance Mustang for the street that also possessed a racing heart because it was primarily created for NASCAR homologation purposes. Among these, the BOSS 429 stands out as perhaps the most impressive Mustang ever. 

Under its hood was a 7.0-liter V-8, the largest engine to ever grace a Mustang. While officially rated at <375ps>, its true output was said to be closer to <600ps>. And the car's signature hood scoop came only on the Boss 429.
DescriptionLong.0x00007F71:
Since it was founded in 1948, Porsche has continually represented the highest level of automotive performance in both motorsports and on the public road. The Porsche Vision Gran Turismo honors the virtues of the German manufacturer with a future version of a sports car designed without restrictions. 

Merging elements many historic Porsches from the past with those of today, including the 919 Hybrid super car and the company's first EV, the Taycan, the Porsche Vision Gran Turismo may well be the closes thing to the perfect sports car. 

Virtually built around a state-of-the-art carbon monocoque chassis, the cabin is enclosed by a glass dome. Powering the car are dual electric motors that combine to produce 820 kW (<1114ps>) and 1090 Nm (<111kgm>) of torque. An innovative active aerodynamic system dynamically reacts to all driving situations to enhance the car’s performance. 

The car's styling was inspired by past Porsche race cars such as the 908 and the legendary 917, and while the Porsche Vision Gran Turismo looks like it belongs exclusively on a track, it was created to also shred winding roads as a true GT car.
DescriptionLong.0x00007F72:
Alongside the Z and the GT-R, the Silvia (240SX) represented one of Nissan's most prominent sports cars. The seventh-generation Silvia (S15) was introduced in January 1999 with a smaller body than its predecessor and a focused sport-car-minded disposition. 

Under the S15's hood was the SR20 engine, which also powered the S13 and S14, but tuned for enhanced performance. The naturally aspirated version produced <165ps> and <19.6kgm> of torque, while the turbocharged inline-4 pumped out <250ps> and <28.0kgm>. The S15 came in two trim levels: the Spec S and the Spec R, which also came with a manual 6-speed gearbox. 

While sharing the same basic chassis of the S13 and S14, the new Silvia boasted a stiffer body structure, better braking performance and upgraded suspension system. It also featured a helical LSD that made it a much better handler then the S14. 

The Spec R was the choice for enthusiasts, thanks partly to a weight-to-power ratio of <4.96kg/ps>. In 2000, a convertible model, the Varietta, was introduced with a naturally aspirated engine, but the entire line was discontinued just two years later, marking the end to this legendary model after 38 years.

*This model was specially tuned to meet Gr.4 regulations by Gran Turismo.
DescriptionLong.0x00007F7F:
The 205 Turbo 16, a Group B car developed by Peugeot for the World Rally Championship, was similar to the production 205 in both looks and name, but it was an entirely different animal on the inside.

Built on a pipe frame chassis, the 205 Turbo was a converted mid-engine car, with its turbocharged 1.8-liter inline-4 that produced more than <350ps> placed where the rear seats once were. The engine sent power to all four wheels, while its double wishbone suspensions system at all four corners provided incredibly agile handling. To better access to the engine and rear suspension for maintenance, the rear half of the body shell from the B-pillar back was a single fiberglass piece that could be lifted out of the way.

The car made its racing debut at the 1984 Tour de Corse. That year it won three races and followed it up in 1985 with three more. But because Peugeot wasn't satisfied with those results, it manufactured an extra limited run of 20 specially modified cars.
